chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Building Your Practice Lab
chapters.partTitle: Part 0 — standing up the virtual machines you will practise on
chapters.exam: RHCSA (EX200) — no direct objective; this is the lab everything else runs in
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: Why build a lab at all
concepts.main: Every command in this book is safe to try only on a machine you built yourself and can throw away.
simple: Think of it as a practice room. You learn to drive a car by driving badly on a closed track first, not in live traffic.
If you practise `rm -rf` or a bad partition table on a real machine, there is no undo. On a cloned VM, you snapshot and restore in a minute.
parts: isolated virtual machines on your own workstation.
a wrong command on a real server is permanent.
mistakes cost you a snapshot restore, not a rebuild.
concepts.remember: Practise only where a mistake is cheap.

concepts.title: The network plan
concepts.main: You decide the addresses up front, on paper, so every machine can be built without guessing later.
simple: Write down each machine's name, its address, and which network it sits on before building anything.
Keeping a written plan is what stops you giving two machines the same address an hour in.
parts: the first network — your workstation and two servers.
the second network — reached only through the router.
the jump host; the router sits on both networks.
concepts.remember: Plan the addresses on paper first; guessing later causes duplicates.

sections.title: Part 2 — Getting RHEL and building the machines

concepts.title: Getting RHEL for free, legitimately
concepts.main: Red Hat offers free subscription routes that give you the real RHEL, not a rebuild.
simple: You do not need to buy anything to learn on the genuine product. Red Hat publishes free subscription options specifically for developers, students and individual use.
It matters that it is the real RHEL: the files, paths and behaviour you practise are the ones you will meet on the job.
parts: a free account that gives access to real RHEL packages.
what you practise matches production behaviour.
concepts.remember: The free subscriptions give you genuine RHEL — not a lookalike rebuild.

concepts.title: Build one machine, then clone it
concepts.main: You install RHEL once into a 'gold' machine and clone it, because installing five times is slow and gives five slightly different machines.
simple: Make one perfect machine. Take copies of it for everything else.
This guarantees all your lab machines behave identically, and it takes minutes rather than an afternoon per machine.
example: take 4 clones from the same snapshot
parts: the one you install and configure properly, once.
a copy of it — fast, and identical every time.
consistency, and five installs become one.
concepts.remember: Install once, clone many — that is what makes the lab fast and consistent.

concepts.title: The one thing this lab cannot reproduce
concepts.main: A lab of virtual machines has no real hardware failures, so some skills can only be read, not practised here.
simple: You cannot pull a real disk out of a virtual machine. Disk failure, some hardware faults and true physical cabling are outside what a lab can teach.
Knowing the boundary is useful: it tells you which skills need real hardware later, instead of assuming you are covered.
concepts.remember: A lab cannot teach real hardware failure — know where its limits are.

revision: Build one machine, clone the rest
chapters.inOneSentence: Plan the addresses, install RHEL once into a gold machine, clone it, and snapshot — then practise freely because mistakes are cheap.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Getting Started with Red Hat Enterprise Linux
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 1 — what Linux is, what RHEL adds, and why the community rebuilds differ
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

sections.title: Why learn Linux, and what makes it different

concepts.title: Why bother learning Linux
concepts.main: Linux quietly runs most of the internet, most cloud instances and almost all networking equipment you rely on.
simple: When you open a website or use an app, a Linux server is very likely answering. That includes the routers, firewalls and phones around you.
Learning it is learning the machine most systems are actually built on.
concepts.remember: Most of what the internet is made of runs on Linux.

concepts.title: Three traits that made Linux everywhere
concepts.main: Open source, runs on everything, and free of per-seat licence costs.
simple: Anyone can read the code, change it, and give the changes back. That means problems get fixed by many people instead of one vendor.
It runs on anything from a phone to a room-sized server. And because there is no licence fee per machine, running thousands of copies costs nothing extra.
parts: anyone may read, change and redistribute the code.
same system on a phone and on a server.
running 1 or 10,000 machines costs the same licence-wise.
concepts.remember: Open source, runs everywhere, no per-seat cost — that is why Linux won.

concepts.title: From kernel to distribution
concepts.main: The kernel manages hardware; a distribution is the kernel plus everything else you need to actually use it.
simple: The kernel is the engine — it controls memory, processes and hardware. On its own it is not a usable system.
A distribution bundles the kernel with the installer, the package manager, the text editor, the shell and thousands of tools, all tested together.
Think of the kernel as the engine and the distribution as the whole car.
parts: hardware, memory and process scheduling — the engine.
kernel + installer + tools, tested together — the whole car.
Red Hat's distribution, sold with a support contract.
concepts.remember: The kernel is the engine; the distribution is the whole car.

concepts.title: RHEL versus the community rebuilds
concepts.main: RHEL is the original commercial product; CentOS Stream, Rocky and AlmaLinux rebuild its source freely, with trade-offs in support and release timing.
simple: Rebuilds compile the same source packages Red Hat publishes. The code is largely the same.

The difference is around it: Red Hat provides a tested combination with a support contract and a defined lifecycle. Rebuilds are free, but you get no Red Hat support and sometimes a slightly different release schedule.
parts: the original, with a support contract and defined lifecycle.
free, compiled from the same source, no Red Hat support.
tracks *upstream* — it shows what will be in the next RHEL, not what is in the current one.
concepts.remember: Rebuilds are free and near-identical, but you get no Red Hat support.

revision: shows what is coming in the NEXT RHEL
chapters.inOneSentence: The kernel is only the engine; RHEL is the whole tested car with a support contract, and the rebuilds are free copies with the same code but no support.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Accessing the Command Line
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 2 — the shell, the prompt, and working efficiently in Bash
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: What the shell is
concepts.main: The shell is the program that reads what you type and runs it.
simple: The shell sits between you and the kernel. You type a command; the shell works out which program you mean, runs it, and shows you the output.
RHEL's default is bash, the GNU Bourne-Again Shell.
parts: the text showing who you are and where you are.
user, hostname, current directory, then # for root or $ for a normal user.
concepts.remember: The shell reads your command and runs it; # means root, $ means normal user.

concepts.title: How a command is put together
concepts.main: Every command has the same three parts: the command, its options, and its arguments.
simple: Like a sentence: the command is the verb, options are adverbs, arguments are the nouns it acts on.
Once you see this pattern, every command looks like every other command.
parts: an option — how to do it.
an argument — what to do it to.
concepts.remember: command + options + arguments — the same shape every time.

concepts.title: Logging in over the network
concepts.main: ssh user@host gives you a remote shell as if you were sitting at that machine.
simple: The same account and password works, but the keyboard and screen are the other machine's. Everything after you log in is identical.
From a lab workstation this is how you reach servera and serverb.
parts: the account to log in as.
concepts.remember: ssh user@host puts you at that machine's keyboard, not on a different system.

concepts.title: The shortcuts worth memorising
concepts.main: A few keys save more time in an exam than anything else you could learn.
simple: Most of these are not exam objectives on their own, but each one turns a slow, error-prone sequence into one or two keystrokes.
example: !$            last argument of the previous command
Tab           complete a filename or command
Ctrl+a / Ctrl+e   jump to start / end of the line
Ctrl+u        delete from cursor back to the start
parts: the single biggest time-saver — complete instead of typing.
search your whole command history by typing part of it.
get out of a command that is waiting for input.
concepts.remember: Tab to complete, Ctrl+r to search history, Ctrl+c to escape — those three pay for themselves.

concepts.title: Understanding history expansion
concepts.main: The shell keeps your commands, and ! lets you reuse them without retyping.
simple: Typing `!!` re-runs the previous command. Typing `!$` inserts the last argument of the previous command, which saves retyping long paths.
parts: the list of what you have run.
the last argument of the previous command.
concepts.remember: !! repeats the last command, !$ reuses its last argument.

chapters.inOneSentence: The shell runs what you type; every command is verb + options + nouns; and Tab, Ctrl+r and Ctrl+c are the shortcuts that buy back the most time.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Managing Files from the Command Line
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 3 — paths, creating and removing files, links, and shell expansions
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: The file-system hierarchy
concepts.main: Everything starts at one root directory, /, and everything else hangs from it.
simple: There is no drive letter and no C:. One top folder, and every file and folder lives somewhere below it.
It is a single tree, which is why an absolute path always begins with /.
parts: the root — the one folder everything starts from.
variable data — logs and caches that change.
concepts.remember: One root, /, and every path starts from it.

concepts.title: Absolute versus relative paths
concepts.main: An absolute path starts at the root; a relative path starts where you already are.
simple: Absolute paths are like a full street address. Relative paths are like 'two streets past the bakery, turn left' — they only work from one starting point.
The dot . means 'here' and two dots .. mean 'the folder above'.
parts: absolute — the full address from the root.
relative — the same file only if you are already in /etc.
the parent directory — one level up.
return to the directory you were in last.
concepts.remember: Absolute starts at /, relative starts at where you are.

concepts.title: Creating and copying
concepts.main: touch makes an empty file, mkdir makes a folder, and cp copies one to another.
simple: Three separate verbs for three separate jobs. Learning them apart saves guessing.
parts: create an empty file if it does not exist.
with mkdir, create parent folders too instead of failing.
concepts.remember: touch for files, mkdir for folders, and -p builds the path.

concepts.title: Moving and renaming
concepts.main: mv both moves a file and renames it, depending on what you point it at.
simple: One command does two jobs. If the destination is a new name in the same place, it renames. If it is a folder, it moves.
concepts.remember: mv renames when the target is a new name, moves when it is a folder.

concepts.title: Removing files and folders
concepts.main: rm removes files, rm -r removes folders and their contents.
simple: rm does not ask. There is no 'are you sure' and no undo — a deleted file is gone unless it is a snapshot.
This is the command to slow down and re-read before pressing Enter.
parts: delete a folder and everything in it.
force — suppress the prompt that could save you.
both together: no prompt, recursive, immediate.
concepts.remember: rm -rf deletes permanently with no confirmation and no undo.
concepts.warning: There is no confirmation prompt and no undo on rm. Read the path twice. In a lab, snapshot first.

concepts.title: Hard links versus soft links
concepts.main: A hard link is another name for the same file; a soft link is a shortcut that points at it.
simple: A hard link is like giving someone a second key to the same door. The file has not moved and neither copy can tell it is a copy — delete one and the data is still there.
A soft link is a signpost. It stores only the path. If the original file is deleted or moved, the signpost points nowhere.
This is the important difference: hard links break when the file is renamed; soft links break when the file is deleted or moved.
parts: create a hard link — a second name for the same data.
create a soft link — a shortcut storing a path.
shows the inode; two hard links share one inode number.
the data stays, because another name points to it.
if the target is removed or moved, the link points to nothing.
concepts.remember: Hard link = same data, survives deletion; soft link = a path, breaks if the target moves.

concepts.title: Pattern, brace and variable expansion
concepts.main: The shell can expand * and ? into filenames, {a,b} into lists, and $NAME into values — before the command even runs.
simple: Your command never sees the asterisk. The shell replaces it with matching filenames first, then runs the command on the results.
Globbing matches names. Brace expansion builds lists of anything — it is not limited to files.
parts: brace expansion — builds a comma-separated list.
brace expansion — builds a numeric range.
command substitution — use a command's output in place.
concepts.remember: The shell expands globs and braces before the command runs — never type a literal * you did not mean.

concepts.title: Quoting and why it matters
concepts.main: Quotes stop the shell from expanding things. Use them whenever a name contains a space or a special character.
simple: Without quotes the shell sees each space as a separate argument and each * as a wildcard.
With quotes the shell hands the text to the command exactly as you typed it.
parts: everything is literal — no expansion at all.
keeps spaces together but still expands $ and *.
the shell splits on spaces and expands wildcards.
concepts.remember: Quote anything with a space or a * in the name.
concepts.warning: An unquoted variable holding a path with spaces turns one argument into two, and the command fails in a confusing way.

revision: cp -r SRC DEST  /  mv SRC DEST
chapters.inOneSentence: One root tree; absolute and relative paths; touch/mkdir/cp/mv/rm; hard links are the same data while soft links are just a path; and quote anything with a space.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Getting Help in RHEL
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 4 — man pages, info pages and apropos
chapters.exam: RHCSA (EX200) — 1.6 use documentation and help systems
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: The man page
concepts.main: Every real command has a manual page, and reading one properly answers almost any question.
simple: You do not need to memorise flags. You need to know how to look one up in ten seconds, which is what the man page teaches.
In an exam or on the job, the man page is always available — using it is a skill, not cheating.
parts: show the manual page for a command.
the fifth section is a file format, not a command.
inside the page, type / then the word to jump to matches.
jump to the next or previous match.
search all man pages for a keyword (apropos).
concepts.remember: man COMMAND, then / to search inside it and q to quit.

concepts.title: The man page sections
concepts.main: The numbered sections each describe a different kind of thing, so you know which one to ask for.
simple: Commands and file formats both have man pages, so they are numbered to keep them apart. When you are not sure, try the likely section.
parts: file formats — the structure of a config file.
read the structure of /etc/fstab, not a command called fstab.
concepts.remember: Section 1 is commands, 5 is file formats — use the number when a name could be either.

concepts.title: GNU Info documentation
concepts.main: info covers deeper material than man does, and is used mainly for GNU core tools.
simple: Man pages are short by design. When you want the full manual, info has it — mostly for tools that came from the GNU project.
It uses a menu you navigate with arrows rather than scrolling.
concepts.remember: man for the quick answer, info when you need the full story.

chapters.inOneSentence: man COMMAND gives the quick answer, / searches inside it, man -k finds commands by keyword, and info holds the deeper manuals.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Creating, Viewing and Editing Text Files
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 5 — streams, pipelines, Vim, and shell variables
chapters.exam: RHCSA (EX200) — 2.4-2.6 streams, pipelines and text editing
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: Standard input, output and error
concepts.main: Every command has three channels: it reads from 0, writes results to 1, and writes errors to 2.
simple: Think of three labelled tubes. Most commands only use one, but all three are always there.
This is why you can take a command's normal output and feed it somewhere else — the output is just a stream you can redirect.
parts: where a command reads its input.
write stdout to a file, replacing it.
write stderr to a file instead.
send both into the same file.
concepts.remember: 0 in, 1 results, 2 errors — and 2>&1 merges errors into the results.

concepts.title: Pipelines and tee
concepts.main: A pipe sends one command's output straight into the next command as its input.
simple: Like a conveyor belt: the output of the first machine becomes the input to the second. No temporary file needed.
tee splits the stream — it sends it onward down the pipe and also writes a copy to a file.
parts: pipe — feed one command's output into the next.
write a copy to FILE while still passing it down the pipe.
redirect a file into a command's stdin instead of the keyboard.
concepts.remember: Pipe with |; use tee when you want to save a copy and keep processing.

concepts.title: Here documents
concepts.main: A here document feeds several lines of text into a command as its input.
simple: Useful when a command needs multiple lines and you do not want to create a file first — writing a short config, for instance.
parts: start feeding lines until you type EOF on its own line.
must match the opening word exactly.
concepts.remember: << EOF ... EOF feeds multi-line text to a command.

concepts.title: Vim has modes, and that is the whole difficulty
concepts.main: Vim behaves differently depending on its current mode.
simple: This is why new users get stuck: pressing a letter in the wrong mode does something unexpected instead of typing it.
Learn the modes first and Vim stops being mysterious.
parts: the default — navigate and run commands. Press Esc to return here.
actually typing text. Enter with i, a, o or I.
open a new line below and start typing.
concepts.remember: Esc returns to Normal mode; i/a/o enter Insert mode; :wq saves and quits.

concepts.title: Getting unstuck in Vim
concepts.main: There is a small set of keys that rescue you from almost any Vim situation.
simple: Almost every 'Vim has frozen' problem is one of these: you are in Insert mode and cannot run a command, or you have unsaved changes and :q will not work.
parts: back to Normal mode — always safe.
if you are truly lost, this leaves Vim without saving.
concepts.remember: Esc, then :q! to bail out safely — that gets you unstuck every time.

concepts.title: Shell variables versus environment variables
concepts.main: A shell variable lives only in your current shell; an environment variable is passed to every command you run.
simple: A shell variable is a note on your desk. An environment variable is pinned to the door, so everyone who walks in can read it.
Commands only see environment variables — that is why HOME and PATH work everywhere without you passing them.
parts: assign, with no spaces around the =.
make it visible to every command you run.
show them with their export status.
concepts.remember: A plain assignment is shell-only; export passes it to your commands.

concepts.title: PATH and why it decides which command runs
concepts.main: PATH is an ordered list of folders; the shell runs the first match it finds.
simple: Imagine the shell checking a list of drawers in order and using the first one holding the tool you asked for.
If an older copy of a command sits in an earlier folder, that one runs — which is why a newly installed command sometimes seems to be ignored.
parts: colon-separated list of folders, searched left to right.
show every match found in PATH.
append a folder — $PATH first so you keep the existing ones.
concepts.remember: PATH is searched left to right; the first match wins — which is the answer to 'I installed it but nothing changed'.

chapters.inOneSentence: Every command has three streams you can redirect; pipes chain them; Vim is mode-based and Esc always rescues you; and only exported variables reach your commands.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Managing Local Users and Groups
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 6 — accounts, superuser access, passwords and account restriction
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: Why every process has a user
concepts.main: Every running program belongs to a user, and every file is owned by a user — that ownership is the basis of all Linux security.
simple: Because each process has an identity, the system can answer one question for any action: who is asking?
Permissions then decide what that identity may do. Identity plus permissions is the whole model.
parts: the superuser, root. One UID, unlimited power.
reserved for services; never for people.
concepts.remember: Every process and every file has an owner — identity is the basis of all permissions.

concepts.title: Primary and supplementary groups
concepts.main: Every user has one primary group, and can belong to any number of extra groups.
simple: Your primary group is your main team — it owns files you create. Supplementary groups are extra teams you are a member of.
This is why `id` is more informative than `whoami`: it shows all of them at once.
parts: show your own UID and every group you belong to.
shown as 'group' — owns new files you create.
only your username — less informative than id.
concepts.remember: One primary group owns your new files; supplementary groups just add access.

concepts.title: Do not log in as root directly
concepts.main: Red Hat's guidance is to log in as a normal user and escalate only when you actually need to.
simple: Working as root all the time means one typo is a system-wide problem. Log in as yourself, and step up briefly for the specific thing that needs it.
It also gives you a record of which account actually ran sudo.
concepts.remember: Log in as a normal user and escalate only when needed.

concepts.title: The four ways to get a root shell
concepts.main: su, su -, sudo, and sudo su - each get you root, but they differ in environment and accountability.
simple: The difference matters: `su` without a dash keeps some of your old environment, which can quietly change how commands behave. The dash gives you root's clean environment.
sudo records who asked for elevation. su on its own often does not.
parts: become root with root's environment (the dash is what matters).
run one command as root, and it is logged.
start a root login session — logged, and with a clean environment.
become root — becomes root, which may not be logged the way you expect.
concepts.remember: The dash in su - gives a clean environment; sudo leaves an audit trail.

concepts.title: Managing user accounts
concepts.main: A small set of commands covers creating, modifying and deleting accounts.
simple: Learn this table. Nearly every account question is answered by one row of it.
parts: create a user AND its home directory. -m matters.
add a user to an extra group.
delete the user and their home directory.
concepts.remember: useradd -m creates the home directory; usermod -aG adds a group.

concepts.title: The -aG trap
concepts.main: usermod -G without -a replaces the user's supplementary groups instead of adding to them.
simple: This quietly causes the exact problem it looks like it should fix: you add one group, and every other group they belonged to is erased.
The 'a' stands for append. Always use it.
parts: ADDS to the existing groups — what you almost always want.
concepts.remember: Always usermod -aG. Without the a, you wipe the user's other groups.
concepts.warning: Forgetting -a silently removes every other supplementary group the user had.

concepts.title: Where passwords actually live
concepts.main: /etc/passwd holds the account details; the encrypted password is in /etc/shadow, which only root can read.
simple: Splitting them means ordinary users can read the account list without ever being able to see password hashes.
Nine colon-separated fields, and the second one in shadow is the hash.
parts: the encrypted password plus aging data — root only.
show a user's password age and expiry.
concepts.remember: passwd for the accounts, shadow for the hashes — that split is the security.

concepts.title: Locking, unlocking and expiring
concepts.main: You can lock an account, unlock it, and set when a password must be changed.
simple: Locking does not delete anything — it just stops the password working, and the shell can be changed so the account cannot be used at all.
Forcing an expiry is a normal way to demand a password change at the next login.
parts: lock the account (prefixes the hash with !).
force a password change at the next login.
force change after this many days.
minimum age, maximum age, warn days.
concepts.remember: passwd -l locks, -u unlocks, -e forces a change; chage -M sets the policy.

revision: Create a user with a home dir
chapters.inOneSentence: Every process and file has an owner; log in as yourself and escalate with sudo; and useradd/usermod/userdel with -m and -aG cover almost every account task.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Controlling Access to Files
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 7 — permissions, ownership, special bits and umask
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: Reading an ls -l line
concepts.main: Every file has one owning user, one owning group, and permissions for three categories: user, group, other.
simple: The nine characters after the first are three groups of three, in a fixed order: user, group, other — and within each, read, write, execute.
parts: the file type — - file, d directory, l symbolic link.
read, write, execute for the owner.
read and execute for the group.
concepts.remember: -rwxr-x--- reads left to right as type, owner, group, other — each with rwx.

concepts.title: Which permission actually applies
concepts.main: The most specific match wins: if you are the owner, the owner permissions apply — even if you are also in the group.
simple: This is the rule people get wrong most often. There is no falling back to the group permissions if the owner ones are restrictive.
The system checks user first, then group, then other, and stops at the first match.
example: # bob is in staff, but the file is alice's, so bob gets NOTHING
parts: are you the owner? then owner permissions apply — stop.
are you in the owning group? then group permissions apply — stop.
concepts.remember: Check owner first, then group, then other — the first match wins and there is no fallback.
concepts.warning: Being in a file's group grants you nothing if you also happen to be the owner and the owner bits are restrictive.

concepts.title: Directories need execute, files need read
concepts.main: Execute on a directory means you may enter it and list it — it is the 'right of way' through a folder.
simple: For a file, x means 'run it as a program'. For a directory, x means 'you may come in'.
Without directory execute, listing the contents fails even with directory read.
parts: enter it, and reach files inside.
create, delete or rename entries inside it.
concepts.remember: Execute on a directory is the right of way — without it, read does nothing.

concepts.title: chmod in octal
concepts.main: Each category is a digit where read is 4, write is 2 and execute is 1.
simple: Add the numbers up. 7 is 4+2+1 (everything), 5 is 4+1 (read and execute), 6 is 4+2 (read and write).
Once the three digits are familiar, you can read any permission string at a glance.
parts: owner full, group read, others read — the common default.
owner only, nobody else — right for private keys.
owner full, everyone else read+execute — right for scripts and directories.
concepts.remember: 4 is read, 2 is write, 1 is execute — add them up per group.

concepts.title: chmod in symbolic form
concepts.main: You can add, remove or exactly set permissions by naming who and what.
simple: Think of it as a sentence: who, then do what, then what to. u g o for who, + - = for what.
parts: take write away from the group.
concepts.remember: chmod WHO WHAT WHICH — u/g/o/a then + - =.

concepts.title: chown and chgrp
concepts.main: chown changes the owner, chgrp changes the owning group — and only root may give a file away.
simple: Ownership is a separate thing from permissions — changing one does not change the other.
Only root can set a file's owner to a different user. Changing the group is allowed for any file you own.
parts: recurse into a whole directory tree.
clear the group and use the user's login group.
concepts.remember: chown changes owner, chgrp changes group, -R goes through a whole tree.

concepts.title: The three special permission bits
concepts.main: setuid, setgid and the sticky bit each change how a file or directory behaves for whoever uses it.
simple: They are not about access at all — they change behaviour. That is the difference worth remembering.
You can spot them in ls -l where an ordinary rwx becomes s, S, or t.
example: chmod 2775 dir     # setgid on a directory
parts: a program runs with the OWNER's privileges, not yours.
new files inside inherit the DIRECTORY's group.
a program runs with the GROUP's privileges.
in a shared directory, only the owner may delete their own files.
how they appear: lowercase s means the bit is set AND execute works.
concepts.remember: setuid = run as the owner; setgid on a dir = inherit its group; sticky = only the owner can delete.
concepts.warning: A capital S means setuid is set but execute is NOT — the program would not run anyway.

concepts.title: umask and default permissions
concepts.main: New files and folders start from a fixed baseline, then your umask removes permissions from it.
simple: The baseline is 666 for files and 777 for directories. Your umask is subtracted from that baseline.
So a umask of 022 turns 666 into 644, and 777 into 755 — which is why almost everything you create is 644 or 755.
parts: private: files 600, directories 700 — right for keys.
show the mask in symbolic form instead of digits.
concepts.remember: umask is subtracted from 666 for files and 777 for directories.

revision: owner first, then group, then other — first match wins
chown USER:GRP file   /   chgrp GRP file
chapters.inOneSentence: Every file has one owner and one group; the first matching permission set wins with no fallback; 4/2/1 make the digits; and umask is subtracted from 666 or 777.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Monitoring and Managing Linux Processes
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 8 — processes, job control, signals and load
chapters.exam: RHCSA (EX200) — 5.1-5.4 monitoring and modifying process behaviour
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: Every running program is a process
concepts.main: A process is a program in motion: it has its own memory, its own identity, and a Process ID.
simple: The program is the recipe; the process is a cook following that recipe. You can have ten processes running the same program, each with separate memory and its own PID.
The PID is how every tool refers to a specific running process.
parts: the process ID — how you refer to one running process.
the parent process that started it.
the common full listing — all users, all processes.
concepts.remember: The program is the recipe; the process is one cook following it, with its own PID.

concepts.title: The process states
concepts.main: The STAT column tells you what a process is doing right now.
simple: Most processes are S and that is fine — S means sleeping, waiting for something. Only a few states need your attention.
parts: running or ready to run — using CPU right now.
sleeping — waiting for something. Normal and harmless.
uninterruptible sleep — almost always waiting on disk I/O. A long D is a hardware or storage problem.
zombie — finished, but the parent has not collected it yet.
concepts.remember: R is running, S is normal sleep, D is waiting on disk, T is stopped, Z is a zombie.

concepts.title: Running things in the background
concepts.main: Adding & runs a command in the background and gives you your prompt straight back.
simple: Useful when something takes a while — a download, a long report — and you want to keep working meanwhile.
It is one job, running independently of your prompt.
parts: bring job N back to the foreground.
send a stopped job back to the background.
suspend the foreground job, stopping it.
concepts.remember: & backgrounds it, jobs lists it, fg brings it back, Ctrl+Z suspends it.

concepts.title: What a signal is
concepts.main: A signal is a software interrupt delivered to a process — a polite message telling it something.
simple: It is how the kernel and other processes talk to a running program. Most signals are a request to stop, and a well-written program shuts down cleanly.
Sending the right signal is how you stop things properly rather than forcing them.
parts: please stop — the polite request. Try this first.
the kernel kills it immediately. It cannot be caught, blocked or ignored.
hang up — daemons traditionally use it to reload config.
suspend, cannot be caught or ignored.
concepts.remember: SIGTERM (15) asks politely; SIGKILL (9) cannot be refused, caught or ignored.

concepts.title: kill and pkill
concepts.main: kill sends a signal to a process by PID, and pkill selects targets by name or attribute.
simple: Always try 15 first. Only escalate to 9 if the process refuses — SIGKILL gives the program no chance to clean up, which can leave corrupted data.
pkill is faster but blunter: it can match more than you intended.
parts: signal every process matching a name.
signal every process belonging to a user.
concepts.remember: kill -15 first, kill -9 only as a last resort — 9 skips cleanup entirely.
concepts.warning: SIGKILL gives the process no chance to close files or flush buffers. That is how you cause corruption.

concepts.title: Reading the load average
concepts.main: Load average counts how many processes want the CPU, sampled at 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
simple: Think of a queue at a counter. One number means one process waiting, three means three waiting, and it rises when work arrives faster than it can be done.
It is not a percentage. On a 4-CPU machine, a load of 4 is fully busy, and higher means things are queueing.
parts: recent demand — reacts fast, can be noisy.
the long trend — best for spotting a real problem.
load above the number of CPUs means work is waiting.
the quickest place to read it.
refresh every second — shows runnable and blocked processes.
concepts.remember: Load is a queue length, not a percentage — compare it to your CPU count.

concepts.title: Finding what is using the CPU
concepts.main: top shows live CPU and memory use per process, and sorts by the column you choose.
simple: It is the first place to look when something is slow. Press P to sort by CPU, M by memory.
top and ps are answers to different questions: top is right now, ps is the full picture.
parts: in top, press Shift+P to sort by CPU.
concepts.remember: top for right now, ps for the whole picture; Shift+P sorts by CPU.

revision: top   (Shift+P = CPU, M = memory, q = quit)
R running  S sleep  D disk-wait  T stopped  Z zombie
chapters.inOneSentence: A process is a running instance with its own PID and memory; signals are how you stop them politely with 15 before forcing with 9; and load is a queue length to compare against your CPU count.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Controlling Services and Daemons
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 9 — systemd units, and starting, stopping and reloading
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: A daemon and a unit
concepts.main: A daemon is a background service; systemd manages it through a unit file.
simple: A service that answers requests while you do something else is a daemon — sshd, chronyd, firewalld.
systemd tracks each one with a unit, which is a text file describing how to start, stop and restart it.
parts: a background service that keeps running.
the file systemd uses to manage it.
listens for connections and starts the service on demand.
schedules a unit, often with a .service beside it.
concepts.remember: A daemon is the running service; the unit is the file systemd uses to control it.

concepts.title: Viewing service state
concepts.main: systemctl status shows whether a unit is running, and systemctl is-enabled says whether it starts at boot.
simple: Two different questions: is it running now, and will it start on the next boot? Both matter and they are often confused.
The coloured word in systemctl status tells you which: active, inactive, failed, enabled.
parts: it tried to start and did not work — go and read the log.
it will not start at boot.
blocked entirely, cannot be started at all.
concepts.remember: is-active is now, is-enabled is at boot — different questions.

concepts.title: Comparing start, restart and reload
concepts.main: reload asks the service to re-read its config; restart stops it and starts it again.
simple: Reload is gentle — the service keeps running and just re-reads its settings. Restart interrupts it, so existing connections drop.
Using reload where it works is better for a live server, because nothing using the service notices.
parts: stop then start — interrupts existing connections.
control whether it starts at boot.
do the boot action AND start/stop immediately in one command.
block a unit completely / undo that.
concepts.remember: reload is gentle and keeps connections; restart interrupts them; enable --now does both boot action and start.

concepts.title: Editing unit files the safe way
concepts.main: Never edit a vendor unit directly — override it under /etc/systemd/system/ instead.
simple: Package updates replace files under /usr/lib/systemd/system/. Anything you write in /etc/systemd/system/ survives and takes priority.
systemctl edit creates the override for you, with a merge block at the top.
parts: vendor files — package updates overwrite these.
create an override without touching the vendor file.
remove overrides and go back to the vendor file.
tell systemd to re-read unit files after editing.
concepts.remember: systemctl edit creates the override under /etc — never hand-edit /usr/lib.

chapters.inOneSentence: systemd manages daemons through unit files; is-active is now while is-enabled is at boot; reload is gentle where restart interrupts; and systemctl edit keeps you out of vendor files.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Configuring and Securing SSH
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 10 — host keys, key authentication and hardening sshd
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: Host keys and that first prompt
concepts.main: Every SSH server has a host key that identifies it, and your client records it the first time you connect.
simple: Like a fingerprint. If a machine's fingerprint changes, you are no longer talking to the same machine — which is exactly what an interception attempt looks like.
Never accept a changed fingerprint without knowing why it changed.
parts: the server's permanent identity, stored in /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*_key.pub.
the client's record of fingerprints it trusts.
you are being asked to confirm that identity — read the fingerprint.
the client has never seen this host before.
something is wrong — or the host key was legitimately regenerated.
concepts.remember: The host key is the server's fingerprint — a changed fingerprint is a warning, not something to click through.

concepts.title: How key authentication works
concepts.main: A public key on the server verifies a private key you keep locally, so no password ever crosses the network.
simple: The private key stays on your machine and never leaves it. The public key sits in a file on the server saying which keys may log in.
The server sends a challenge, your private key signs it, and the public key checks the signature. The password is never involved.
parts: the private key — never copy or share this.
the public key — this is what goes on the server.
copy your public key and append it to the account's authorized_keys.
on the server, the list of public keys allowed to log in.
concepts.remember: The private key stays on your machine; only the public key goes on the server.

concepts.title: Permissions that break SSH
concepts.main: OpenSSH refuses keys and some files when their permissions are too loose.
simple: It is strict on purpose: if anyone else could read your private key or modify authorized_keys, they could log in as you.
This is the single most common cause of 'my key is being ignored'.
parts: the private key must not be group or world readable.
else another user could add their own key.
sshd silently ignores the key and falls back to password.
concepts.remember: chmod 700 ~/.ssh and 600 on both keys — sshd silently ignores keys that are too open.
concepts.warning: If permissions are wrong, ssh does not say so clearly; it just ignores the key and asks for a password.

concepts.title: Generating a key with a passphrase
concepts.main: A passphrase encrypts the private key on disk, so a stolen key file is useless without it.
simple: Think of it as a second lock on the safe holding the key. Slightly slower to use, far safer if the laptop is ever lost.
parts: a label stored in the public key to identify it.
set an empty passphrase — less safe.
KDF rounds when setting a passphrase.
concepts.remember: A passphrase encrypts the private key on disk; ed25519 is the modern type to use.

concepts.title: Turning off password authentication
concepts.main: Once keys work, you can stop accepting passwords entirely, which removes the brute-force surface.
simple: This is the single biggest SSH improvement. With keys working first, switching passwords off costs you nothing and closes the most attacked door.
Do not do it until you have confirmed you can log in with a key in a second terminal — otherwise you can lock yourself out.
parts: stop root logging in over SSH directly.
key login stays enabled — check this is on.
only these accounts may log in.
concepts.remember: PasswordAuthentication no is the biggest win — but test your key login first, or you lock yourself out.

concepts.title: Validating the config before reloading
concepts.main: sshd can check its configuration and tell you about errors without starting.
simple: A typo in sshd_config can leave the service unable to start at all, which on a remote machine means you cannot log in to fix it.
Testing first is the difference between catching a typo and being locked out.
parts: test the config — reports syntax errors, starts nothing.
dump the effective settings after all defaults are applied.
do not reload — fix the error first.
concepts.remember: sshd -t before every reload — a typo you cannot see is how you lock yourself out.
concepts.warning: Never restart sshd over a remote connection without testing the config first. You may not be able to log back in.

chapters.inOneSentence: The host key is the server's fingerprint; key auth keeps the private key local and only the public key on the server; and sshd -t before every reload, because a typo can lock you out.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Analyzing and Storing Logs
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 11 — systemd-journald, rsyslog, journalctl and time
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: journald and rsyslog are not the same thing
concepts.main: systemd-journald collects everything into the journal; rsyslog additionally writes the traditional text log files.
simple: Two services, two different jobs. journald is the modern structured store that most things write to. rsyslog is the older text-file system that tools and older software still expect.
Both run by default. When a log is missing from /var/log, this split is usually why.
parts: collects everything systemd and services report.
writes /var/log/messages, secure, cron and the rest.
the journal on a RAM-backed filesystem — lost on reboot.
the journal on disk — survives reboot.
concepts.remember: journald collects everything; rsyslog writes the text files in /var/log.

concepts.title: Querying the journal
concepts.main: journalctl reads the journal, and can filter by time, unit, priority, PID and more.
simple: It replaces grepping through log files. Because the journal is structured, you can filter on the fields directly rather than matching text.
parts: filter by severity: emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug.
follow new messages live — the one to leave running.
this boot only; -b -1 is the previous boot.
concepts.remember: journalctl -f to follow live, -u for a unit, -p for severity, -b for this boot.

concepts.title: Making the journal survive a reboot
concepts.main: If the journal lives on /run it is memory-backed and gone on reboot; moving it to /var/log makes it persistent.
simple: Compare the two paths. If /var/log/journal exists you already have a persistent journal; if only /run/log/journal exists, logs vanish on reboot.
Persistent logs are what you need when investigating something that happened before a crash or reboot.
parts: memory-backed — lost on reboot. The RHEL default.
set in journald.conf to make it permanent.
concepts.remember: /run/log/journal is lost on reboot; /var/log/journal persists.

concepts.title: Log rotation and the usual text files
concepts.main: Old logs are compressed and rotated so they do not fill the disk.
simple: logrotate renames the current file, compresses it, and starts a new one. The rotated files stay as .1, .2.gz and so on.
Knowing which file holds what saves hunting: secure is logins, messages is everything routine, cron is scheduled jobs.
parts: the tool that rotates, compresses and prunes old logs.
the policy telling it when and how long to keep.
concepts.remember: secure for logins, messages for routine, cron for scheduled jobs.

concepts.title: Why accurate time matters more than it sounds
concepts.main: Logs from different machines are only comparable if their clocks agree.
simple: When you are reconstructing what happened across several servers, mismatched clocks make the sequence a guess.
Authentication also depends on time — expired certificates and Kerberos both fail if the clock is wrong.
concepts.remember: Logs are only comparable when the clocks agree — time is a security dependency, not just bookkeeping.

concepts.title: chrony and timedatectl
concepts.main: chrony keeps the clock synchronised, and timedatectl shows the current time settings.
simple: The system asks an upstream time server what the time should be and corrects itself gradually, rather than jumping the clock.
Gradual correction matters: a sudden jump backwards can confuse running services.
parts: show and set the system's time and time zone.
how closely the clock is tracking.
which time sources are being used and whether they agree.
set by name, not by offset — Asia/Dhaka, not +06:00.
the alternative time service on newer systems.
concepts.remember: chrony corrects gradually rather than jumping the clock; set time zones by name.

chapters.inOneSentence: journald collects everything and rsyslog writes the text files; journalctl filters by unit, severity and boot; and a journal under /run is lost on reboot.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Managing Networking
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 12 — TCP/IP, addressing, NetworkManager and name resolution
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: The four layers in plain terms
concepts.main: Data moves down the layers on one machine, across the wire, and back up on the other.
simple: Each layer only talks to the layers beside it. Your application hands data to the transport layer, which labels it; the internet layer addresses it; the link layer physically sends it.
On the receiving machine the same thing happens in reverse. This is why a problem at one layer does not affect the others — and why each has its own diagnostic tool.
parts: how programs talk to each other — ssh, https, NFS.
the actual hardware on this network — ethernet, MAC addresses.
concepts.remember: Application → transport → internet → link, and each layer has its own tools.

concepts.title: Reading an IPv4 address and prefix
concepts.main: An address splits into a network part and a host part, and the prefix length says where the split is.
simple: Think of a street address: 'this street, number 42'. The prefix says which part names the street and which names the house.
/24 means the first 24 bits are the network — so the last octet is the host.
parts: the first 24 bits are network — the last octet identifies the host.
usable hosts .1 to .254; .0 is the network, .255 is the broadcast.
concepts.remember: /24 means the last octet is the host — .0 is the network and .255 is the broadcast.

concepts.title: IPv6 in brief
concepts.main: IPv6 is 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hex digits, and RHEL runs both at once.
simple: The address space is enormously larger — enough for every device ever made, rather than nearly exhausted.
Dual-stack means IPv4 still works alongside it, so nothing breaks during the transition.
parts: compresses runs of zero groups — the full form may be very long.
IPv4 and IPv6 both active by default.
fe80:: addresses exist on every interface.
concepts.remember: IPv6 is 128 bits, :: compresses zero groups, and RHEL is dual-stack by default.

concepts.title: ip commands
concepts.main: ip configures interfaces and addresses, and ss shows what is listening and what connections exist.
simple: These are the modern replacements for the older ifconfig and netstat, which are deprecated and may not be installed.
Learn these names rather than the old ones.
parts: every interface, its state and its MAC address.
the routing table — how traffic leaves.
listening sockets and connections, with process names.
the old names — deprecated, may be missing.
concepts.remember: ip for configuration, ss for sockets — ifconfig and netstat are the old names.

concepts.title: ping and tracepath
concepts.main: ping tests reachability, tracepath shows the path.
simple: Ping answers 'can I reach it and does it answer?'. Tracepath answers 'which routers does my traffic actually cross?' — which is how you find where a connection breaks.
parts: send N packets then stop, instead of running forever.
pinging a name shows the address it resolved to.
show each hop toward the destination.
concepts.remember: ping tests reachability, tracepath shows the route, and ping -c stops after N packets.

concepts.title: NetworkManager owns the configuration
concepts.main: You do not edit network files directly — you tell NetworkManager what you want and it writes the files for you.
simple: Think of NetworkManager as the only person allowed to rearrange the furniture. Edit its files by hand and the next reload silently overwrites you.
nmcli is how you give it instructions.
example: nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name work ifname ens160 ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.101/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1
parts: list hardware devices and their state.
use the address you supply, not DHCP.
the address and prefix to set.
a device is the hardware; a connection profile is the saved settings.
concepts.remember: Never hand-edit network files — tell NetworkManager via nmcli, it owns them.
concepts.warning: A hand-edited connection file will be overwritten the next time NetworkManager reloads its settings.

concepts.title: Changes take effect in two places
concepts.main: Setting a profile's values does not apply them — you must also bring the connection up.
simple: nmcli connection modify changes the saved profile. nmcli connection up applies it.
Forgetting the second half is the most common reason a change appears to be ignored.
parts: change the saved profile only — nothing changes yet.
re-read profiles from disk after editing files.
concepts.remember: modify saves, up applies — do both or nothing happens.

concepts.title: Setting the hostname and hosts file
concepts.main: The hostname identifies the machine; /etc/hosts maps names to addresses locally.
simple: The DNS server is the public phone book. /etc/hosts is your private one-page list for local machines.
hostnamectl or hostnamectl sets the name permanently — plain `hostname` only changes it until reboot.
parts: local name-to-address mapping, checked before DNS.
resolve using the real system order, hosts then DNS.
concepts.remember: hostnamectl sets it permanently; /etc/hosts is your local list; getent shows the real resolution order.

revision: ip link show   /   ip addr show
nmcli device status   /   nmcli connection show
nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name NAME ifname DEV ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses A/P
chapters.inOneSentence: Data moves application → transport → internet → link; ip configures and ss inspects; NetworkManager owns the files so use nmcli; and remember modify saves while up applies.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Archiving and Transferring Files
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 13 — tar, compression, scp, sftp and rsync
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: What an archive contains
concepts.main: A tar archive holds the files' data plus their metadata plus an index, in one file.
simple: Think of packing a whole drawer into one box, including a list of what's inside. Because the index travels with the data, you can pull out one member without unpacking everything.
parts: the archive filename — almost always required.
verbose: show each file as it works.
change directory before doing the work.
concepts.remember: tar -c creates, -x extracts, -t lists — and -f FILE names the archive.

concepts.title: Compression is a separate flag
concepts.main: tar bundles, gzip compresses — the flags combine both in one step.
simple: Bundling many files and shrinking them are two different jobs, joined by different letters.
Forgetting -z on extract is a common cause of 'it will not unpack'.
example: tar -cJf archive.tar.xz dir    # xz, best ratio
parts: the compression flag on extract must match the one used to create.
concepts.remember: -z gzip, -j bzip2, -J xz — and the extract flag must match the create flag.

concepts.title: The leading-slash message
concepts.main: tar strips leading slashes so an archive cannot overwrite your system by accident.
simple: When you archive an absolute path, tar prints 'Removing leading /' and stores it relative.
That message is a safety feature, not an error. It is why an extracted archive lands in the current directory rather than overwriting /.
parts: tar is protecting you — the paths were stored relative.
preserve absolute paths. Dangerous — only when you truly mean it.
are the safe default, and why restores land where you cd to.
concepts.remember: 'Removing leading /' is tar protecting you, not an error.
concepts.warning: -P preserves absolute paths and can overwrite your system on extract. Do not use it casually.

concepts.title: scp and sftp
concepts.main: Both run over SSH, so they use the same keys and the same encryption as your login.
simple: Wherever ssh already works, these already work — no extra setup, no separate password.
scp copies; sftp gives you an interactive file transfer session, similar to an old ftp but encrypted.
parts: the remote side — the colon is what makes it remote.
concepts.remember: scp copies over SSH with the same keys as your login; the colon marks the remote side.

concepts.title: rsync
concepts.main: rsync sends only the differences between the source and the destination.
simple: scp copies every byte every time — fine for a small file, wasteful for a large tree. rsync compares first and transfers only what changed.
That is why rsync is the right tool for repeated syncs of the same directory.
parts: archive mode: recurse and preserve permissions, times, symlinks.
dry run — show what would happen without doing it.
remove destination files that are gone from the source.
on /data/ copies the contents; on /data copies the folder itself.
concepts.remember: rsync -a preserves and transfers only differences; a trailing slash decides whether the folder or its contents are copied.
concepts.warning: --delete removes destination files that no longer exist in the source. Dry-run with -n first.

chapters.inOneSentence: tar -c/-x/-t bundle and unpack with -f naming the file; compression is a separate flag that must match; and rsync -a transfers only what changed.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Installing and Updating Software Packages
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 14 — subscriptions, RPM, dnf, repositories and modules
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: Registering the system
concepts.main: Registering attaches a Red Hat subscription to the machine so it can reach the official repositories.
simple: Until it is registered, the machine cannot download packages from Red Hat's servers — so this comes before any dnf install.
The username and password are the ones from your subscription account, not the root password.
parts: attach a subscription — needed before dnf can fetch anything.
detach it, e.g. when snapshotting a lab VM.
concepts.remember: Register before installing — until then the official repositories are out of reach.

concepts.title: What an RPM actually holds
concepts.main: An RPM packages files together with metadata: name, version, dependencies, licence, and a scriptlet history.
simple: The metadata is why rpm -q --whatprovides works: the package manager knows every file it installed, which is how you trace a config file back to its package.
Know the query flags — they answer most package questions instantly.
parts: which package owns this file? The reverse lookup.
which package provides this file — works even for a file no package has installed.
not installed — for rpm -q this is a valid answer, not an error.
concepts.remember: rpm -qf FILE answers which package owns a file; exit code 1 from rpm -q just means not installed.

concepts.title: Why you use dnf rather than rpm
concepts.main: dnf understands repositories and resolves dependencies for you; rpm installs only the single file you name.
simple: rpm asks you to work out the dependency order yourself. dnf reads the repository, works out the whole set of packages needed, and installs them together.
In daily use you almost always want dnf.
parts: bring installed packages up to their newest available version.
details, including which repository offers it.
search for which package provides a file — the dnf answer to rpm -qf.
a log of every transaction dnf performed.
concepts.remember: dnf resolves dependencies across repositories; rpm installs only the one file you name.

concepts.title: CURRENCY: dnf, not dnf5
concepts.main: On RHEL 10 the daily tool is still dnf; the separate dnf5 package is not installed by default.
simple: Some RHEL 9 and 10 documentation refers to dnf5, which is a different, faster implementation. It is available as a separate package.
This was confirmed by observation on a live RHEL 10.2 host: dnf 4.20.0 is present and dnf5 is not installed. Use dnf.
parts: the installed tool on the verified RHEL 10.2 host.
a separate package, not installed by default.
for the exam and for normal administration.
concepts.remember: RHEL 10 ships dnf, not dnf5 — dnf5 is a separate package you would have to install.

concepts.title: Managing repositories
concepts.main: A repository is a source of packages; dnf only uses the ones you enable.
simple: Think of a shopping list. A disabled repository is a shop you are not allowed into — its packages simply do not exist as far as dnf is concerned.
Repository files live under /etc/yum.repos.d/.
parts: extra content not enabled by default.
concepts.remember: repolist --all shows everything; disabled means dnf pretends it does not exist.

concepts.title: Application Streams and modules
concepts.main: Application Stream splits large software into separately versioned streams, so you can run several versions side by side.
simple: Without modules you would have to choose one version of, say, PostgreSQL for the whole system. Modules let each application pick its own version.
That is what removes the classic dependency conflict where two applications need different major versions of the same thing.
parts: the way back out if you lock in the wrong stream.
concepts.remember: Modules let different applications use different major versions of the same software.

revision: dnf module list / enable NAME:STREAM / reset NAME
chapters.inOneSentence: Register to reach the official repositories; rpm knows which package owns which file while dnf resolves dependencies across repos; and modules let two apps use different major versions of the same software.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I
chapters.title: Accessing Linux File Systems
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 15 — block devices, mounting, and finding files
chapters.exam: RHCSA (EX200) — 12.1-12.3 mounting file systems and finding files
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: One directory tree for every disk
concepts.main: Linux attaches every storage device into a single directory tree, so there are no drive letters.
simple: Unlike Windows, adding a disk does not create a new letter. Its contents appear as a folder inside the existing tree.
The folder where a device appears is its mount point.
parts: names for disks depending on the bus type.
a partition on the first SATA/SCSI disk.
show devices, sizes and mount points as a tree.
also show filesystem type and UUID.
show UUID and filesystem type without mounting.
concepts.remember: Every disk joins the one tree at a mount point — lsblk shows what is attached where.

concepts.title: Mounting and unmounting
concepts.main: mount attaches a filesystem at a folder; umount detaches it.
simple: The folder must exist before you mount into it — create it first or mount fails.
You cannot unmount a folder that is in use. That single rule causes most 'device is busy' errors.
parts: attach a filesystem at a folder.
specify the filesystem type, e.g. -t nfs.
show what is mounted where — easier to read than mount output.
something is using the folder — cd out and close files there.
concepts.remember: Create the mount point first; umount fails while anything is using the folder.
concepts.warning: Unmounting a filesystem with unmounted-but-busy data risks losing writes. Close everything under the mount point first.

concepts.title: UUIDs and persistent mounts
concepts.main: Naming a mount by device path is fragile; naming it by UUID survives hardware changes.
simple: Device names like /dev/sdb can change between boots depending on detection order. A UUID is assigned to the filesystem itself and does not move.
That is why /etc/fstab entries are written with UUID= on a modern system.
parts: a permanent identifier stored inside the filesystem.
a name the kernel assigns — it can change between boots.
read the UUID of a device.
concepts.remember: Mount by UUID in fstab — device names can change, UUIDs do not.

concepts.title: find versus locate
concepts.main: find walks the filesystem live; locate looks up a pre-built index and is instant but may be out of date.
simple: Imagine searching every room in the building (find) versus reading a directory list someone compiled yesterday (locate).
A file you created two minutes ago is in the building but not on yesterday's list — which is why find finds it and locate does not.
parts: silence the permission errors you will get searching /.
concepts.remember: find searches live and is always right; locate is instant but needs updatedb after new files.

concepts.title: Useful find combinations
concepts.main: find is most powerful when you combine tests and actions.
simple: Two or three tests narrow it to exactly what you want, and -exec or -delete then acts on the results.
Start narrow rather than piping to grep afterwards.
parts: listing tests one after another means all must match.
run a command on each result; {} is the filename.
delete the matches — try without it first.
limit how deep to search — much faster.
concepts.remember: Combine tests to narrow it down; use -maxdepth for speed and -delete carefully.

chapters.inOneSentence: Every disk joins the one tree at a mount point, mount by UUID because device names move, and find searches live while locate is instant but can be out of date.

chapters.partTitle: Chapter 16 — Web Console, the Customer Portal and Red Hat Insights
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: A browser-based admin interface
concepts.main: Web Console gives you a graphical interface to the server over HTTPS on port 9090, without installing a desktop.
simple: Useful when you want to look at a server from a laptop, or when you do not want to put a desktop on a headless machine.
It is not installed by default and it does not start until you enable it.
parts: the socket unit that activates it.
start it and make it start at boot.
or the browser simply cannot connect.
concepts.remember: Web Console is not installed by default, needs enable --now, and must be allowed through firewalld.

concepts.title: The Red Hat Customer Portal
concepts.main: access.redhat.com holds documentation, knowledgebase articles, downloads and support cases.
simple: The knowledgebase is where a documented fix for a specific error message usually lives, which is faster than searching the web.
A support case needs a valid subscription.
parts: articles indexed by error message — search the message, not the symptom.
support tickets, requiring an active subscription.
concepts.remember: Search the knowledgebase by the literal error message, not by a description of the problem.

concepts.title: Red Hat Insights
concepts.main: Insights runs a lightweight client that uploads configuration metadata so Red Hat can flag problems before they happen.
simple: It checks your running configuration against Red Hat's knowledge of what breaks, and tells you about issues affecting that particular combination of versions.
It uploads metadata about the system, not your data. That distinction is worth being clear about.
parts: configuration facts, not your application data.
clear the data with insights-client stop and clear.
proactive warnings about known issues affecting your version mix.
concepts.remember: Insights uploads configuration metadata, not your data, and warns about issues affecting your exact version combination.

chapters.inOneSentence: Web Console gives a browser admin UI on 9090 but must be installed and enabled; the knowledgebase is searched by exact error message; and Insights reads configuration metadata, not your data.
