chapters.partTitle: Chapter 17 — objectives map, command reference, practice scenario and exam-day checklist
chapters.source: RH124 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration I)

concepts.title: The highest-yield commands
concepts.main: A small set of commands answers a large share of the exam.
simple: If you only have time to be fluent with a limited set of tools, these give the most coverage per minute spent.
Knowing one command thoroughly beats half-knowing five.
concepts.remember: Be fluent with this list before learning anything rarer.

concepts.title: Working a practice scenario
concepts.main: Real administration problems arrive as a story: several machines, a complaint, and something to make work.
simple: The skill being tested is ordering: gather facts first, identify the actual cause, change the minimum, then verify.
Changing several things at once leaves you unable to say which one mattered.
parts: read the error, check status and logs, look at the config.
find the cause, not the nearest-looking thing.
prove the symptom is gone, do not assume it.
note what you changed and why.
concepts.remember: Gather, identify, change one thing, verify — in that order, every time.

concepts.title: Exam-day habits
concepts.main: Time management and reading questions carefully decide more marks than obscure knowledge.
simple: Mark questions you cannot answer quickly and come back. A stuck question costs the easy ones behind it.
Read what the question asks you to do — 'list' and 'show' want different outputs.
parts: answer everything you can do quickly.
do not burn five minutes on one item.
return to the marked ones with the time left.
list, show, configure — they want different things.
check a changed service actually works, do not just that it started.
concepts.remember: Mark what you cannot do and come back — a stuck question costs you the easy ones behind it.

revision: ls -l, find, systemctl, chmod, useradd -m, rpm -qf, journalctl, nmcli
gather -> identify -> change one thing -> verify
first pass quick, mark the rest, return at the end
chapters.inOneSentence: Be fluent with a dozen high-yield commands, work problems by gathering first and changing one thing at a time, and on exam day mark what you cannot do rather than getting stuck.

chapters.bookTitle: RHEL Administrator Part 2
chapters.title: Improving Command-Line Productivity
chapters.partTitle: Chapters 1 and 2 combined — scripts, loops, conditions, regular expressions and job scheduling
chapters.source: RH134 course material (RHEL Administrator Part 2)

concepts.title: What a shell script is
concepts.main: A Bash script is a text file holding a list of commands that Linux runs in sequence.
simple: Imagine a checklist for your morning server check. Instead of retyping the same commands every day, you write them once and run the file.
The shell reads the file line by line and runs each line exactly as if you had typed it.
parts: the shebang — tells the kernel which interpreter reads the file.
a comment — the shell ignores it.
concepts.remember: A script is a saved list of commands, run in order, exactly the same way every time.

concepts.title: Specifying the interpreter
concepts.main: Without a shebang, the shell falls back to /bin/sh, which is more limited than Bash.
simple: Bash has features that plain sh does not — arrays, [[ ]], process substitution. If your script starts failing on syntax you are sure is correct, the interpreter is the first thing to check.
The shebang removes the guesswork by naming the interpreter explicitly.
parts: run with Bash — what you almost always want.
run with plain sh — portable but limited.
the shell defaults to sh when you run it, which can behave differently.
concepts.remember: Always start a Bash script with #!/bin/bash — without it you silently get sh.

concepts.title: Executing a script
concepts.main: A new file must be made executable before you can run it by name.
simple: The file is just text until you give it permission to be a program. That permission is the execute bit.
parts: run the file in this folder. The ./ means 'here'.
run it with Bash explicitly — no execute bit needed, though arguments still pass correctly.
concepts.remember: chmod +x, then ./name — or bash name if you do not want to change permissions.

concepts.title: Quoting special characters
concepts.main: Without quotes the shell interprets spaces, asterisks and dollar signs itself before the command ever sees them.
simple: When you type rm $file the shell expands $file first, and rm receives whatever it became. That is convenient until the value contains a space, and then rm receives two arguments instead of one.
Quotes hand the text to the command exactly as you typed it.
parts: keep it as one argument, but still expand $ and *.
everything literal — no expansion at all.
the shell splits on spaces and expands wildcards.
concepts.remember: Quote anything containing a space or a wildcard — and quote variables.
concepts.warning: rm $file unquoted becomes rm $file1 $file2 if the variable holds two names, and removes the wrong things.

concepts.title: Providing output
concepts.main: echo prints values, and quoting it stops the shell from mangling them.
simple: echo "Total: $count files" prints a readable line. But echo is not perfectly safe with backslashes and some special values — printf '%s\n' is the stricter alternative.
The practical rule: quote what you echo, and use printf when the text matters.
parts: print a line — convenient, but interprets some escape sequences.
print exactly, with no interpretation — safer for values.
concepts.remember: Quote your echo arguments; use printf when the exact text matters.

concepts.title: Why loops exist
concepts.main: A loop runs the same block of commands once for every item in a list.
simple: Administration is full of repetition: check ten servers, process every file in a folder, restart three services.
Write the command once and let the loop do the repeating.
example: for HOST in host1 host2 host3; do
parts: take each item from LIST, one at a time.
the start and end of the repeated block.
concepts.remember: for X in LIST; do ... done runs the block once per item.

concepts.title: Providing lists to a loop
concepts.main: The list can be typed, generated from a range, matched from filenames, or produced by another command.
simple: Knowing which source to reach for is the actual skill. A brace range builds numbers, a glob matches filenames, and command substitution takes the output of another command.
example: for H in host1 host2; do ... done       # typed
for H in host{1..3}; do ... done       # brace range
for F in /var/log/*.log; do ... done  # glob
for U in $(cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd); do ... done  # command substitution
parts: brace expansion — builds a range of numbers.
glob — matches files by name pattern.
command substitution — the output becomes the list.
concepts.remember: Braces build numbers, globs build filenames, $() builds from a command's output.

concepts.title: Checking several servers
concepts.main: The common real-world loop: run the same check across a list of hosts over SSH.
simple: You almost never inspect ten machines one at a time. The loop does the repetition and the command does the check.
The single quotes around the remote command matter — they stop the local shell from expanding the remote variables before they are sent.
example: for HOST in servera serverb; do
parts: connect to each machine in turn.
single quotes so the remote shell, not the local one, interprets it.
concepts.remember: A loop over hosts plus SSH is how you check many machines without typing each one.

concepts.title: Understanding exit codes
concepts.main: Every command reports success or failure as a number: 0 means success, anything else means failure.
simple: This is how a script knows whether the previous step worked. It is not an error message — it is a status, and scripts are built on it.
The special variable $? holds the exit code of the command you just ran.
parts: the command was not found — a very common one.
the exit code of the previous command.
concepts.remember: 0 is success; $? holds the last exit code and is how scripts decide what to do next.

concepts.title: Testing with operators
concepts.main: The && and || operators run a second command only if the first succeeded or failed.
simple: Instead of writing an if statement for a simple chain, you can join commands directly.
This reads like a sentence: 'do this, and only if that worked, do this'.
parts: run B only if A succeeded.
run B only if A failed.
chains get unreadable past two — use an if statement beyond that.
concepts.remember: && runs on success, || runs on failure — useful for short chains, not for long logic.

concepts.title: if / then and if / then / else
concepts.main: An if statement runs a block only when a condition is true, and else covers the other case.
simple: When a chain of && becomes hard to read, this is the readable form. It is the core of every decision in a script.
parts: what to do when it is false.
closes the if — easy to forget.
true if the path is a directory. -f file, -e exists.
concepts.remember: if [ test ]; then ... fi — and fi closes it.

concepts.title: if / elif / else
concepts.main: elif chains multiple tests and stops at the first one that matches.
simple: Like a series of questions asked in order. The first true condition wins, and everything after it is skipped.
Using elif rather than a chain of separate if statements means only one branch can ever run.
parts: greater than / less than / equal to — numbers need -eq, not =.
all matching branches would run — usually not what you meant.
concepts.remember: elif stops at the first true condition; separate if statements would all run.

concepts.title: What a regular expression is
concepts.main: A regular expression describes a pattern of text rather than one exact word.
simple: A normal search looks for a literal string. A regex describes a shape — 'any digit', 'the word error at the start of a line', 'five to ten characters'.
This is what turns reading a huge log file by eye into a single command.
parts: quotes stop the shell from interpreting the pattern.
concepts.remember: A regex describes a pattern, not a literal word.

concepts.title: Anchors, character classes and repetition
concepts.main: ^ and $ pin to line boundaries, [ ] match one of a set, and + * ? control repetition.
simple: These four tools cover most real log searching on their own.
parts: start and end of a line.
any single character from the set.
one or more / zero or more / optional.
an escaped dot — a literal dot, not any character.
concepts.remember: ^ $ anchor, [ ] is a set, + * ? repeat — and escape a literal dot.

concepts.title: Useful grep options
concepts.main: A few options turn grep from a toy into the tool you will use every day.
simple: Counting matches, ignoring case and searching in context are what you actually need when investigating.
parts: invert — show lines that do NOT match.
lines of context before / after the match.
concepts.remember: -c counts, -i ignores case, -v inverts, -B/-A give context, -r recurses.

concepts.title: One-time jobs with at
concepts.main: at schedules a command to run once at a future time; atd is the service that runs it.
simple: Setting an alarm for something later. You type the command, press Ctrl+D to submit, and the job waits.
Use at for a single job at a specific time — not for anything repeating.
parts: show the saved detail of job 28.
concepts.remember: at is for one-time jobs; atq lists them and Ctrl+D submits.

concepts.title: Recurring jobs with cron
concepts.main: crond runs jobs repeatedly on a schedule, and crontab manages your own list.
simple: An alarm that rings every morning instead of once. cron is the service, cronie is the package, crontab is the command you use.
Enter one job per line and save.
parts: the background service that runs the jobs.
concepts.remember: Use crontab for your own recurring jobs; check with -l before -r.
concepts.warning: crontab -r removes every job for the current user with no confirmation and no undo.

concepts.title: The five time fields
concepts.main: The first five fields say when to run; everything after is the command.
simple: They always mean the same five things in the same order. Read left to right before deciding when a job fires.
concepts.remember: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week — then the command.

concepts.title: Cron symbols
concepts.main: Symbols describe repeating times without a separate job for every one.
simple: * is any value, - is a range, , selects specific values and */n is an interval.
Weekdays run 0 or 7 for Sunday through 6 for Saturday, and names like Mon and Jan also work.
concepts.remember: * any, - range, , selected, */n interval.

concepts.title: The day-field OR rule
concepts.main: When BOTH day fields are restricted, cron runs the job when EITHER matches — not when both do.
simple: This surprises nearly everyone. It is an OR, not an AND.
If you need both to be true, run twice, or use a script that checks the date itself.
parts: 12:15 PM on the 15th of the month OR on any Friday.
it does not require both conditions at once.
concepts.remember: When both day fields are restricted, cron uses OR logic between them.

concepts.title: System-wide cron and Anacron
concepts.main: System entries add a username field, and Anacron lets periodic jobs catch up after downtime.
simple: A personal crontab is yours. A system-wide entry has six fields — the extra one is which account runs the command.
Anacron is for jobs that must happen roughly daily whether or not the machine was awake at the time.
parts: put your own system jobs here rather than editing /etc/crontab.
directories of executable scripts run at those intervals.
catch-up jobs — they run late rather than not at all.
concepts.remember: System cron entries have six parts: five time fields, a username, and a command.

concepts.title: systemd timers and temporary files
concepts.main: A timer decides when to activate a unit, and systemd-tmpfiles manages temporary files by written rules.
simple: The timer is the alarm clock; the service is the worker it wakes. They are separate units.
Temporary files need a written policy for what to keep and what to remove — systemd-tmpfiles applies it.
parts: activate an interval after the last activation.
tell systemd to reread unit files after editing.
start at boot AND start now.
apply the creation and removal rules at boot.
remove files past their configured age, now.
concepts.remember: The timer decides when, the service decides what; put custom units under /etc and reload systemd.

chapters.inOneSentence: Scripts save steps so they repeat identically, loops run them over a list, exit codes and if/then decide what happens next, regex finds the exact line, and at or cron puts it on a schedule.

chapters.bookTitle: RHEL Administrator Part 2
chapters.title: Tuning System Performance
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 3 — tuned profiles and process scheduling priority
chapters.source: RH134 course material (RHEL Administrator Part 2)

concepts.title: What tuned does
concepts.main: tuned applies a whole named bundle of system settings at once, instead of you hand-tuning individual values.
simple: Like choosing a preset on an equalizer rather than moving every slider yourself. Each profile knows which disk scheduler, CPU governor and network settings work well together.
parts: the daemon that applies the profile.
concepts.remember: tuned applies a whole named bundle of settings at once.

concepts.title: Static versus dynamic
concepts.main: A static profile applies settings once; a dynamic profile keeps watching and adjusts as conditions change.
simple: Static is setting the thermostat once. Dynamic is a thermostat that keeps reacting as the room changes.
Dynamic tuning can push hard for a busy task and relax once the system goes idle.
parts: settings applied once, when the profile is selected.
tuned monitors activity and adjusts on the fly.
concepts.remember: static applies once; dynamic keeps adjusting as load changes.

concepts.title: What a nice value does
concepts.main: The nice value decides who gets CPU time first when processes compete.
simple: When there is plenty of CPU, priority barely matters. When CPU is contended, priority decides who is served first.
A lower number means higher priority. A nice process is polite — it gives way to others.
parts: lowest priority — most willing to yield.
start a command at a chosen niceness.
concepts.remember: Lower number = higher priority; higher number = more polite.

concepts.title: The privilege rule
concepts.main: Only root can make a process more important; a normal user can only make their own less important.
simple: You can always volunteer to give your own work away. You cannot take priority that belongs to someone else.
That is why nice -n -5 fails for a normal user but works for root.
parts: lower priority — any user may do this to their own process.
concepts.remember: Lowering a nice number needs root; raising it is always allowed.

chapters.inOneSentence: tuned applies named bundles of settings; a nice value decides who waits for the CPU, and only root may make a process more important.

chapters.bookTitle: RHEL Administrator Part 2
chapters.title: Controlling Access to Files with ACLs
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 4 — POSIX ACLs, default ACLs and administration
chapters.source: RH134 course material (RHEL Administrator Part 2)

concepts.title: The limit of normal permissions
concepts.main: Normal permissions give you three groups — owner, group, everyone else — so they cannot say that one extra person also gets write.
simple: Standard permissions are a door with three keys: the owner, the team, and anyone.
If you need one specific outsider to also have access, those three keys cannot express it. ACLs add named users and groups on top.
parts: a named extra user — here, no access.
the ceiling for all named entries and the group.
concepts.remember: ACLs add named users and named groups on top of owner, group and other.

concepts.title: Setting and removing ACLs
concepts.main: setfacl adds, changes and removes the extra named entries on a file.
simple: You are adding a key to the door, or taking one away. -m modifies, -x removes.
Capital X is deliberate: it gives execute only where it makes sense — directories, or files already executable.
parts: a named user — blank name means the owner.
capital X — execute only if a directory or already executable.
concepts.remember: setfacl -m adds or changes, -x removes one, -b clears all extended entries.

concepts.title: The mask and why entries stop working
concepts.main: The mask is a ceiling on all named entries and the owning group, and it can silently reduce them.
simple: Set the owning group's permissions and you will often see the mask shrink with them, quietly removing access from named users.
The mask is not a permission anyone uses directly; it is a limit the system applies.
parts: the maximum any named entry or the group can have.
the rights a named entry actually has after the mask applies.
concepts.remember: The mask caps named entries — a #effective:rw comment means the mask reduced them.

concepts.title: Default ACLs on directories
concepts.main: A default ACL on a directory is inherited by everything created inside it.
simple: This is how you give a whole project directory the right access once, rather than setting every new file individually.
parts: a default entry — inherited, not applied to the directory itself.
new files pick it up automatically.
concepts.remember: A default ACL on a directory is inherited by everything created inside it.

concepts.title: Copying and moving files with ACLs
concepts.main: cp preserves an ACL only with -a or -p; mv keeps the file and therefore keeps its ACL.
simple: A plain cp drops extended entries unless you ask, and the file then looks like it lost permissions.
parts: does NOT preserve an extended ACL.
keeps the same file, so the ACL travels with it.
concepts.remember: cp drops ACLs unless you use -a or -p; mv keeps them.

chapters.inOneSentence: ACLs add named users and groups on top of owner, group and other; the mask caps them; and a default ACL on a directory is inherited by everything inside it.

chapters.bookTitle: RHEL Administrator Part 2
chapters.title: Managing SELinux Security
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 5 — modes, file contexts, Booleans and troubleshooting denials
chapters.source: RH134 course material (RHEL Administrator Part 2)

sections.title: What SELinux is, and its modes

concepts.title: Why normal permissions are not enough
concepts.main: Standard permissions and ACLs are Discretionary — the owner decides. SELinux is Mandatory — the policy decides, even over root.
simple: Under normal permissions, whoever owns a file hands out access, and any process running as that owner inherits it.
SELinux flips this. A process asks whether the policy allows its type to act on that type. Even root can be refused.
parts: Discretionary Access Control — the owner decides.
Mandatory Access Control — the policy decides, regardless of ownership.
concepts.remember: Owner decides is DAC; system policy decides is MAC, which is SELinux.

concepts.title: The three modes
concepts.main: Enforcing blocks and logs, Permissive only logs, and Disabled turns SELinux off entirely.
simple: Enforcing is a locked door. Permissive is the same door with the lock off — you get through, but it still records what it would have refused.
parts: deny the action and log it.
allow it, but still log the denial.
off — only changeable in the boot configuration.
switch between permissive and enforcing at runtime.
concepts.remember: getenforce shows the mode; setenforce switches it at runtime; /etc/selinux/config sets it at boot.

concepts.title: The SELinux context
concepts.main: Every file, directory and process carries a context of user:role:type:level, and the type decides file access.
simple: Think of the label as a sticker on the file saying what it is. The policy compares your process's type with the file's type.
parts: almost always what matters for file access decisions.
concepts.remember: ls -Z shows the context; the type field is what SELinux actually compares.

concepts.title: How files get their context, and the mv trap
concepts.main: New files inherit their context from the parent directory, but moving a file keeps its original context.
simple: Moving a file carries the old sticker with it, even into a folder that needs a different one. This is the number one cause of it worked yesterday.
parts: KEEPS the original context — the common problem.
takes the new location's default context.
reset a path's contexts back to the policy default.
change a context directly — not persistent across relabel.
concepts.remember: mv keeps the old label, cp takes the new one — and restorecon fixes a wrong label properly.
concepts.warning: A file that works in one directory and is denied in another usually just has the wrong label. Check ls -Z before changing anything else.

concepts.title: Setting a context permanently with semanage
concepts.main: chcon changes a label but is lost on relabel; semanage records a persistent rule instead.
simple: Think of chcon as changing the sticker by hand, and semanage as telling the system that files in this folder should always carry this label.
Because the rule is stored, it survives a relabel and applies to files you have not created yet.
parts: add a rule. The (/.*)? covers the directory and everything under it.
apply the stored rules to files on disk now.
concepts.remember: chcon is temporary; semanage fcontext is the persistent fix, followed by restorecon.

concepts.title: What a Boolean is
concepts.main: A Boolean is a pre-built on/off switch for a known policy variation, and is far safer than custom policy.
simple: Should Apache serve files out of users' home directories? That is one switch — httpd_enable_homedirs — instead of hand-building a rule.
parts: list every Boolean and its state.
change it for THIS boot only.
change it and make it persistent.
concepts.remember: setsebool changes for this boot; setsebool -P also makes it permanent.

concepts.title: A safe troubleshooting order
concepts.main: Start by asking whether SELinux is actually wrong, then check the file context, then a Boolean, and only then write policy.
simple: A web server reading /home might be exactly the attack SELinux exists to stop. Do not reflexively fix every denial.
parts: ask whether SELinux is actually wrong here.
check the file context with ls -Z — fix with restorecon (least risky).
check whether a documented Boolean covers it.
only as a last resort, add a custom rule with audit2allow.
concepts.remember: Fix the label before the Boolean, and the Boolean before writing policy.

concepts.title: Reading a denial
concepts.main: A denial names the source context (the process) and the target context (the file).
simple: Read it as a sentence: a process of this type tried to do this to something of that type, and policy says no.
parts: who was trying — the process, for example httpd_t.
what it wanted — the file, for example default_t.
inspect a denial in detail on a desktop system.
concepts.remember: Read a denial as process type did this to file type — both halves matter.

concepts.title: ausearch and generating a policy
concepts.main: ausearch finds the denial in the audit log, and audit2allow can turn denials into a custom policy module.
simple: ausearch -m avc -ts recent is the command you reach for when you suspect SELinux is blocking something.
audit2allow is a last resort, because a rule generated from a denial you did not understand can lock you out.
parts: search the audit log for SELinux denials.
generate a policy module from the denials found.
concepts.remember: ausearch finds the denial; audit2allow is a last resort, not a first answer.

chapters.inOneSentence: SELinux is a system policy that can refuse even root; check the file context first, then a Boolean, and only write policy as a last resort.

chapters.title: Managing Basic Storage
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 6 — partitioning, file systems, mounts, swap and fstab
chapters.source: RH134 course material (RHEL Administrator Part 2)

concepts.title: Finding and inspecting disks
concepts.main: lsblk shows block devices as a tree with sizes and mount points; lsblk -f adds the file system type and UUID.
simple: lsblk draws the storage as a tree, which is how you see that /dev/sda2 sits on /dev/sda.
parts: disk names depend on the bus type.
a partition on the first disk.
also show file system type and UUID.
concepts.remember: lsblk shows the tree; lsblk -f adds the file system type and UUID.

concepts.title: Creating a partition with parted
concepts.main: parted works interactively or from the command line, and can write a GPT or MBR table.
simple: You are cutting a disk into rooms. Separate partitions mean filling up your data does not fill up the system.
parts: write a GPT partition table — do this first.
start and end points. Starting at 1MiB rather than 0 avoids alignment problems.
tell the kernel to re-read the partition table.
show the layout and the unallocated space.
concepts.remember: mklabel first, then mkpart, then partprobe — and start the first partition at 1MiB.
concepts.warning: partprobe may warn the kernel is still using the table; that is normal and the new partition still appears in lsblk.

concepts.title: Creating a file system
concepts.main: A new partition is empty until you put a file system on it.
simple: Formatting builds the structure inside the partition. Until that happens it is just empty space.
XFS is RHEL's default and the right choice for most new work.
parts: destroys the existing data — there is no undo.
concepts.remember: mkfs.xfs builds the file system; XFS is the RHEL default.

concepts.title: Mounting and making it permanent
concepts.main: mount attaches a file system at a folder, and /etc/fstab makes that happen automatically at boot.
simple: The folder must exist before you mount into it.
fstab is the note the system reads at every startup. Its six columns have a fixed order and getting them wrong is the usual mistake.
parts: what to mount — use UUID= for reliability.
apply everything in fstab — run this right after editing it.
concepts.remember: Create the mount point, mount, then record it in fstab and prove it with mount -a.

concepts.title: Swap space
concepts.main: Swap is disk used as a stand-in for memory when RAM is exhausted.
simple: When RAM fills, the least-used memory moves to swap. It is far slower than RAM, so a machine leaning on swap feels sluggish — but it keeps running.
parts: a swap file should not be world readable.
concepts.remember: mkswap prepares swap, swapon turns it on, swapon --show lists it.

chapters.inOneSentence: Partition the disk, format it, mount it, record it in fstab and prove it with mount -a — and swap follows the same create-then-activate pattern.

chapters.bookTitle: RHEL Administrator Part 2
chapters.title: Managing Logical Volumes
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 7 — LVM concepts, creating and extending volumes
chapters.source: RH134 course material (RHEL Administrator Part 2)

concepts.title: The three layers
concepts.main: LVM separates the physical disks from the volumes you use, so volumes can grow later.
simple: Three layers: physical volumes (real disks), a volume group (a pool spanning them), and logical volumes (the slices you mount).
Because the volumes sit on a pool, you can add a disk to the pool and grow a volume into the extra space without rewriting the data.
parts: physical volume — a real disk or partition prepared for LVM.
volume group — a pool combining one or more physical volumes.
logical volume — a flexible slice of the pool that you format and mount.
list physical volumes, volume groups, logical volumes.
concepts.remember: PV (real disk) -> VG (pool) -> LV (what you mount).

concepts.title: Physical and logical extents
concepts.main: A volume group is chopped into physical extents, and each logical volume is carved from them in logical extents.
simple: The pool is broken into fixed-size chunks; a volume is handed some of those chunks.
That indirection is what lets a volume grow into space added to the pool later.
parts: physical extent — a chunk of the volume group.
logical extent — a chunk given to one logical volume.
PE and LE are normally the same size, so one LE maps to one PE.
concepts.remember: The pool is cut into physical extents; logical volumes are carved from them.

concepts.title: Creating a logical volume step by step
concepts.main: Turn a partition into a PV, add it to a VG, carve an LV, then format and mount it.
simple: Three setup commands in a fixed order, then the same format-and-mount steps as any other file system.
Running them out of order is the usual error — each layer needs the one below it to exist first.
parts: prepare the partition to join LVM.
give it all the remaining free space.
build a file system on the volume.
concepts.remember: pvcreate, then vgcreate, then lvcreate, then mkfs — in that order.

concepts.title: Extending a volume group and a logical volume
concepts.main: Adding a disk to the pool creates free space, which you then hand to a logical volume.
simple: This is the whole point of LVM: the disk underneath changes while the files on top keep working.
Growing the pool only creates room. You must also grow the volume, then the file system inside it.
parts: add a disk into the existing pool.
grow the logical volume AND its file system in one step.
you must run a separate command to grow the file system.
verify the new size is visible.
concepts.remember: vgextend adds space to the pool, lvextend -r hands it to the volume and its file system.

concepts.title: Removing storage safely
concepts.main: A physical volume can only leave the pool if none of its data is still in use.
simple: LVM refuses when removing it would destroy data. That refusal is a protection, not an obstacle.
parts: relocate the data off a physical volume.
take it out of the volume group.
wipe its LVM label so it can be used another way.
concepts.remember: pvmove the data off, then vgreduce, then pvremove.
concepts.warning: Removing a physical volume that still holds live data destroys it. LVM will stop you — read the message rather than forcing it.

chapters.inOneSentence: LVM puts a pool between the disks and the volumes you use, so a volume can grow after the fact by adding a disk to the pool and extending it.

chapters.bookTitle: RHEL Administrator Part 2
chapters.title: Implementing Advanced Storage Features
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 8 — Stratis and VDO
chapters.source: RH134 course material (RHEL Administrator Part 2)

concepts.title: What Stratis adds
concepts.main: Stratis sits on top of LVM and adds its own thin pool, snapshots and checksumming on one file system.
simple: LVM gives you flexible volumes. Stratis manages them as one pool with automatic snapshotting and integrity checking built in.
The checksumming is the real difference: it notices when stored data no longer matches what should be there.
parts: the Stratis pool on top of the block devices.
the usable file system inside the pool.
concepts.remember: Stratis is LVM plus thin snapshots plus built-in integrity checking.

concepts.title: Creating a pool and a file system
concepts.main: You create a pool from block devices, then a file system inside it.
simple: Two steps rather than four — Stratis handles the layers for you.
Then it is mounted like anything else.
parts: build the pool from one or more block devices.
create a file system inside it.
concepts.remember: Create the pool from block devices, then a filesystem inside it, then mount it.

concepts.title: Thin provisioning and snapshots
concepts.main: A thin pool allocates space as it is used, and a snapshot is an instant copy you can roll back to.
simple: Thin provisioning means you can declare a 100 GB file system on a pool holding 20 GB; it fills up only as real data arrives.
A snapshot costs almost nothing because it records what changed rather than copying everything.
example: stratis filesystem snapshot create pool1 fs1 snap1
parts: the declared size, which can exceed the pool.
space is consumed as data is written.
a snapshot lets you return the file system to that moment.
concepts.remember: Thin provisioning declares a size larger than the pool; snapshots are instant and cheap.

concepts.title: What VDO does
concepts.main: VDO compresses data and collapses duplicate blocks before anything is written to disk.
simple: A filing cabinet that squeezes each folder before storing it, and notices when the same paper has been filed twice and stores it once.
Because duplicates collapse, a VDO volume reports a much larger logical size than the disk actually holds.
parts: what the file system sees — usually larger.
the real space taken on the disk.
concepts.remember: VDO compresses and deduplicates, so the logical size is far bigger than the disk use.

concepts.title: Creating a VDO volume
concepts.main: You create the volume against a block device and format the logical device it exposes.
simple: The VDO layer sits underneath a normal file system, so once it exists you mount it exactly like any other.
parts: what the VDO device will be called.
the apparent size presented to the file system.
the device you format and mount.
concepts.remember: Create the VDO volume with physical and logical sizes, then format /dev/mapper/<name>.

revision: stratis filesystem snapshot create pool1 fs1 snap1
chapters.inOneSentence: Stratis gives you a pool with thin snapshots and integrity checking; VDO compresses and collapses duplicates so the logical size far exceeds the real disk use.

chapters.bookTitle: RHEL Administrator Part 2
chapters.title: Accessing Network-Attached Storage
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 9 — NFS and autofs
chapters.source: RH134 course material (RHEL Administrator Part 2)

concepts.title: What network-attached storage is
concepts.main: One computer holds a folder and publishes it; other machines mount it and use it as if it were local.
simple: It is about sharing files, not identity — an NFS mount does not give you a home directory or a shell.
The server exports a folder; the client mounts it and it appears at a normal path.
parts: the machine that exports the folder.
what the server publishes, and to whom.
concepts.remember: The server exports a folder; the client mounts it and it appears as a local path.

concepts.title: NFS versions and why v4 matters
concepts.main: NFSv4 is stateful and uses a single well-known port; earlier versions need extra ports and are stateless.
simple: NFSv3 and earlier bounce through port 2049 plus a range of dynamically allocated ports, which is why firewalling them is fiddly.
NFSv4 uses one port and keeps state, so it is simpler to secure and to mount. Prefer it.
parts: list the shares a server offers.
older, needs many more ports open.
show what is currently mounted and with which options.
concepts.remember: Prefer NFSv4 — one port and stateful, instead of a scatter of ports.
concepts.warning: Mixing versions is a classic source of 'it mounts but I cannot see the files' — check nfsstat -m for which version actually took effect.

concepts.title: Mount options that change behaviour
concepts.main: The options after the comma decide how the client treats the share, especially during a server outage.
simple: The read/write and sync choices are straightforward. hard versus soft is the one that genuinely bites.
hard keeps retrying, which is safe but can freeze your program. soft reports an error instead, which fails fast but can lose a write.
parts: keep retrying when the server is down. Safe, but can hang.
report an error instead of retrying. Can lose a write.
concepts.remember: hard is safer for data; soft fails fast but risks losing a write.
concepts.warning: A hard mount to an unreachable server leaves a program frozen with no way to interrupt it. That is expected behaviour, not a fault.

concepts.title: Server exports
concepts.main: The server must list each folder it offers, who may use it and with which options.
simple: This file is the server's list of what it is willing to share. The client cannot mount anything not exported here.
Run exportfs -a after editing to apply changes without a reboot.
parts: apply every export in the file.
concepts.remember: List the folder in /etc/exports, then run exportfs -a to apply it.

concepts.title: Why use an automounter
concepts.main: autofs mounts a share only when someone uses it, and unmounts it when nobody does.
simple: Instead of keeping ten network shares mounted all day, autofs keeps them ready but idle.
That avoids slow startup and stuck connections from mounting everything permanently.
parts: the service that watches for use and mounts on demand.
start it and make it start at boot.
says which map file defines each mount.
the map file listing the actual shares.
concepts.remember: autofs mounts on first use and unmounts when idle.

concepts.title: Direct and indirect maps
concepts.main: An indirect map puts every share under one directory; a direct map gives each its own mount point.
simple: Indirect: the map file lists server:/path entries, and autofs creates /mnt/nfs/<name> as you cd into them.
Direct: the map file uses full mount points, so /data becomes an automounted mount in its own right.
Indirect is simpler for a set of shares from one server; direct is better when the paths must look exactly as the application expects.
parts: maps a mount point to a map file.
the file lists server:/path; subfolders appear under the mount point.
the file lists the full mount point; each is mounted separately.
the mount happens on access, not at boot.
concepts.remember: Indirect lists shares under one directory; direct gives each its own mount point.

concepts.title: When one user can reach a share and another cannot
concepts.main: An automount that works for root and fails for a normal user is almost always an NFS permission problem underneath.
simple: The mount itself succeeded — automount did its job. What differs is who the files belong to and what permissions they carry.
Anonymous mapping, or simply restrictive ownership on the server, is the usual cause.
parts: show the numeric UID and GID rather than names.
what an unmapped user appears as.
what the files actually belong to.
concepts.remember: If root can reach it and a user cannot, the mount worked — the permissions underneath are the problem.

revision: hard = safe but can hang; soft = fails fast, may lose a write
chapters.inOneSentence: The server exports a folder, the client mounts it with NFSv4, and autofs makes that happen only when someone actually uses the share.

chapters.bookTitle: RHEL Administrator Part 2
chapters.title: Controlling the Boot Process
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 10 — boot sequence, targets, password resets and recovery
chapters.source: RH134 course material (RHEL Administrator Part 2)

concepts.title: What happens when Linux starts
concepts.main: Boot is a fixed sequence: firmware, bootloader, kernel, initial RAM file system, then the real root.
simple: Firmware hands control to the bootloader, which loads a small kernel into memory and gives it a place to find its files — the initramfs, because the real root disk is not ready yet.
The kernel finishes starting, mounts the real root, and systemd takes over.
parts: UEFI or BIOS — chooses the boot device.
loads the kernel and the initramfs.
the core; mounts the root file system.
a small temporary file system used before the real root is available.
starts services and reaches the target.
concepts.remember: firmware -> bootloader -> kernel -> initramfs -> root -> systemd.

concepts.title: Targets and choosing one for a single boot
concepts.main: A target is a named point a group of units can be started or stopped together.
simple: Like station names on a line: reaching the station brings everything scheduled up to that point with it.
You can pick a different one for a single boot without changing the default — that is the safe way to recover.
parts: the normal server state — no desktop.
a minimal environment for repair, with most services.
switch now, without changing the default.
append systemd.unit=TARGET to boot into it once.
concepts.remember: get-default shows the default; set-default changes it; isolate switches now only.

concepts.title: Resetting a lost root password
concepts.main: Interrupt the boot, drop to a rescue environment, and reset the password there.
simple: At the GRUB menu you edit the kernel line to add rd.break, which gives a shell before the real system starts.
That shell runs in a minimal environment with root still read-only, so you remount it read-write, reset the password, then continue.
example: # at GRUB, press e and add to the linux line:
parts: break to a pre-root shell at the GRUB prompt.
move into the real root so passwd edits the real password file.
schedule an SELinux relabel on the next boot.
leave the shell and continue booting.
concepts.remember: rd.break at GRUB, remount rw, chroot, passwd, autorelabel, then boot.

concepts.title: Reading logs from a previous boot
concepts.main: journalctl -b -1 shows the previous boot, which is what you want after a crash or reboot.
simple: After a system restarts, the logs from the failure are in the previous boot's journal.
Without -1 you are only looking at the current boot, which is why the interesting messages seem to have vanished.
concepts.remember: After a restart, the failure is in the previous boot — use journalctl -b -1.

concepts.title: Repairing problems that prevent booting
concepts.main: A wrong /etc/fstab entry drops the system into emergency mode, and the fix is to comment out the bad line.
simple: systemd tries to mount everything in fstab before starting services. If one entry is wrong it refuses to continue.
In emergency mode the root file system is already mounted read-write, so you can edit fstab directly and reboot.
parts: systemd stops before normal start because fstab could not be satisfied.
comment out the failing line, then reboot.
run mount -a after every fstab edit.
a damaged file system may also drop you here; run fsck on the unmounted device.
concepts.remember: Emergency mode usually means fstab — comment out the bad line and reboot.

concepts.title: Emergency mode versus rescue mode
concepts.main: Emergency gives the bare minimum; rescue gives you more of the system plus a comment on why it dropped there.
simple: Rescue mounts your root file system and starts a reasonable set of services; emergency gives almost nothing.
Rescue is the better choice for fixing file system problems, and emergency when you need to change fstab itself.
parts: root mounted, many services running. Use this for file system repair.
the bare minimum. Use this when fstab itself is broken.
boot into either one for a single boot.
concepts.remember: Rescue for file system repair; emergency when fstab itself is the problem.

revision: rd.break -> remount rw -> chroot -> passwd -> touch /.autorelabel
chapters.inOneSentence: Boot runs firmware, bootloader, kernel then systemd; you can break to a shell at GRUB to reset a password; and after a restart the interesting logs are in the previous boot.

chapters.bookTitle: RHEL Administrator Part 2
chapters.title: Managing Network Security
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 11 — firewalld and SELinux port labelling
chapters.source: RH134 course material (RHEL Administrator Part 2)

concepts.title: How firewalld is organised
concepts.main: firewalld manages the firewall using named zones, services and ports, instead of raw rules.
simple: A zone is a group of rules for a type of connection. Instead of writing every port by hand, you tell firewalld which named service you want allowed.
Each interface is assigned a zone, and traffic arriving on it is judged by that zone's rules.
parts: a named set of rules applied to an interface.
a named bundle of ports, like ssh or http.
used by any interface with no zone of its own.
which zone is applied where, right now.
concepts.remember: A zone groups rules for an interface; services are named bundles of ports.

concepts.title: Allowing a service or a port
concepts.main: Allowing a named service is usually better than allowing a raw port, because the service knows the ports it needs.
simple: When you add --add-service=http, firewalld opens the port that http actually uses, and keeps working when that changes.
Adding a raw port is for when there is no named service for what you are running.
parts: allow a named service. Prefer this.
save it so it survives a reload.
the change is temporary and disappears on reload.
concepts.remember: --permanent saves, --reload applies. Forgetting both is why a rule seems to vanish.

concepts.title: Why a service can still be blocked after the firewall allows it
concepts.main: firewalld and SELinux are independent — one opens the port, the other decides whether the process may bind to it.
simple: Opening the port in firewalld lets traffic through the firewall. It does not automatically satisfy SELinux.
If a service starts but refuses to use its port, and the firewall is already correct, the port label is the next thing to check.
parts: controls the label and whether the port may be used.
can stop a service on its own.
concepts.remember: firewalld opens the port; SELinux labels it. A service can be blocked by either one independently.
concepts.warning: A service that starts but will not bind to its port is often a SELinux port label rather than a firewall problem. Check ausearch before opening more ports.

concepts.title: What a port label is
concepts.main: SELinux attaches a type to each port, and a process may only bind to a port carrying a type it is allowed to use.
simple: Think of it as a label on a door. The policy decides which label a service may use, and which port it may bind to.
Running httpd on port 82 fails by default because 82 is not labelled as an HTTP port.
parts: the SELinux type assigned to a port.
the type normally assigned to web ports.
decides which processes may use which type.
concepts.remember: A port label is the SELinux type on a port; the policy decides which processes may bind to it.

concepts.title: Adding, modifying and removing a port label
concepts.main: semanage port assigns a SELinux type to a port, and the change is persistent.
simple: Three commands cover almost everything: list, add, and delete.
Without semanage, fcontext or restorecon a port has no label and most services cannot use it.
parts: list which SELinux type each port carries.
add a label to a port.
concepts.remember: semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp PORT, then restart the service.

chapters.inOneSentence: firewalld decides which ports traffic can reach, SELinux decides which ports a service may bind to — and both can block you independently.

chapters.bookTitle: RHEL Administrator Part 2
chapters.title: Installing Red Hat Enterprise Linux
chapters.partTitle: Chapter 12 — Anaconda, Kickstart and virtual machines
chapters.source: RH134 course material (RHEL Administrator Part 2)

concepts.title: What Anaconda does
concepts.main: Anaconda is the installer — it partitions the disks, installs the packages and configures the system.
simple: It asks you a fixed sequence of questions and then performs the installation from your answers.
Kickstart exists precisely to pre-answer those same questions so the installer never has to ask.
parts: the screen collecting all your choices before anything is written.
concepts.remember: Anaconda asks a fixed sequence of questions and installs from your answers.

concepts.title: Choosing media and verifying it
concepts.main: The ISO must match the CPU architecture, and its checksum should be verified before you trust it.
simple: The installer will not check for you, and a corrupted download fails confusingly halfway through.
Match the architecture — an x86_64 image will not boot on ARM.
parts: a fingerprint of the file; compare it with the published value.
USB or virtual media, not a DVD.
concepts.remember: Verify the checksum and match the architecture before you boot the installer.

concepts.title: The Installation Summary screens
concepts.main: Language, software selection, installation destination, network and root password are the decisions that matter.
simple: Each can be filled in by hand or pre-filled by a Kickstart file.
The disk choice is the one that deserves thought — automatic partitioning can overwrite existing data.
parts: affect the installed system, not just the installer.
where it is written — automatic or manual.
required; a weak one is rejected unless you override it.
concepts.remember: Anaconda asks language, software, disk, network and root password, in that order.

concepts.title: What a Kickstart file is
concepts.main: A Kickstart file answers every installer question in advance so the installation runs unattended.
simple: Imagine writing your answers on a form once and handing the same form to every machine you build.
The installer can fetch it over the network, from a USB stick, or you type its location at the boot prompt.
parts: ordinary text, not a special format.
script sections that run before and after the installation.
the list of packages or groups to install.
told to the installer at the boot prompt.
concepts.remember: A Kickstart file pre-answers the installer; ks=URL tells the installer where to find it.

concepts.title: Post-install scripts and validating the file
concepts.main: The %post section runs after installation and is where anything the standard questions do not cover belongs.
simple: Creating users, writing a config file, enabling a service — none of that has an installer screen, so it all goes in %post.
Validate the file before using it: an error in a Kickstart is much harder to debug than an error in a manual install.
parts: where the new system lives before the first reboot.
move into the new system so commands work on it.
check the file for errors before you rely on it.
concepts.remember: Put anything the installer has no screen for into %post, usually after a chroot — and validate the file first.

concepts.title: Automating disk partitioning in Kickstart
concepts.main: The %pre section runs before installation and is where disk work belongs, because the installer itself manages the disks.
simple: If you need a partition scheme that Anaconda cannot express, you write the partitioning yourself in %pre.
Everything the installer will use must exist before it starts, which is exactly why this step is first.
parts: runs before the installer takes over.
clear and partition in a script.
reuse content from another file or add to it.
concepts.remember: %pre runs before installation — that is where custom disk work belongs.

concepts.title: What virtualization is, and KVM
concepts.main: A virtual machine is a computer defined in software, given its own CPU, memory and disk as a share of the real machine.
simple: It behaves like a separate computer — it runs its own operating system and reboots independently — but it is really a set of files and a slice of the host's hardware.
KVM is the part that talks directly to the processor's virtualisation features; QEMU is the emulator it drives.
parts: the software that runs the guests.
concepts.remember: A VM is a software computer that borrows real hardware from its host.

concepts.title: Preparing a host and verifying support
concepts.main: KVM will not load unless hardware virtualisation is enabled in the firmware.
simple: If KVM is missing, it is usually because VT-x or AMD-V is switched off in UEFI/BIOS rather than anything wrong with RHEL.
Cockpit's Machines tool gives you a browser interface for creating and running guests.
parts: must be enabled in UEFI/BIOS or KVM will not load.
the Cockpit add-on for managing virtual machines.
the libvirt daemon that runs the guests.
concepts.remember: KVM needs VT-x or AMD-V enabled in firmware, otherwise it will not load.
concepts.warning: Do not overallocate memory. A guest assigned more RAM than the host has will fail to start or will freeze the host.

chapters.inOneSentence: Verify the image before booting it; Kickstart answers the installer questions in advance and %pre/%post cover what it cannot; and a VM is a software computer borrowing real hardware from its host.

chapters.title: Comprehensive Review

concepts.title: Review of the course
concepts.main: The chapters build on each other, and the review exists to show you where the gaps are.
simple: Scripts and loops came first because everything later needs them. Storage, then NFS, then boot — each assumes the previous.
A review that you can answer without re-reading is the real measure of what you have learned.
parts: can you do it without notes?
the skipped items become your revision list.
doing it once on a real machine is what counts, not reading it.

concepts.title: Lab 1 — fixing boot issues
concepts.main: Repair a boot failure, fix a bad fstab entry, change the default target and schedule a recurring backup.
simple: This lab deliberately combines several chapters, which is the point: real faults do not arrive neatly labelled.
It is the closest thing in the course to what the exam and real work feel like.
parts: read the status and logs before changing anything.
so you know which change fixed it.
confirm it is genuinely working, not just running.

concepts.title: Lab 2 — file systems and storage
concepts.main: Partition, build an LVM volume, mount it persistently, mount NFS, add swap, and set ACLs.
simple: Almost every storage chapter appears in one exercise, which is what makes it worth doing twice.
The recurring theme is that each layer depends on the one below it being correct first.
parts: create, then make it activate at boot.
the last layer, after the file system is right.
concepts.remember: Storage builds in layers — partition, volume, format, mount, persist — and each layer depends on the last being right.

skipped items are the revision list
