chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III
chapters.title: Why Automate, and What Ansible Is
chapters.partTitle: Part 1 — the control node, inventory, config files and ad hoc commands
chapters.source: RH294 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III)

sections.title: Why automate, and what Ansible is

concepts.title: Why manual administration stops working
concepts.main: One-server-at-a-time administration does not scale, and worse, it does not stay consistent.
simple: By hand, the tenth server gets configured slightly differently from the first — and nobody notices until something breaks.
Automation removes that drift: the same playbook runs identically everywhere, and it is saved in a file you can review and version-control.
It also gives you an audit trail: you can see exactly what was changed, because the change is written down.
concepts.remember: Manual work does not scale and silently drifts; automation is consistent, repeatable and auditable.

concepts.title: Control node and managed nodes
concepts.main: Ansible runs from one control node and applies changes to the managed nodes it targets.
simple: Think of a control tower and the aircraft it directs. You log in to one machine and tell it what should be true everywhere else.
The control node does not need to be a server. Your own workstation is a perfectly normal place to run it from.
parts: the machine where you run ansible-playbook and where the automation lives.
no software installed on the managed node — it talks over SSH.
concepts.remember: One control node drives many managed nodes, over SSH, with nothing installed on the targets.

concepts.title: Ansible modules and idempotence
concepts.main: A module is a small tool that does one job, and modules are written to be idempotent.
simple: Idempotent means: run it ten times and the result is the same as running it once. A module that sets a package to 'installed' does nothing if it is already installed.
That is what makes a playbook safe to re-run — which matters enormously, because re-running is how you recover from a partial failure.
parts: one specific job — install a package, copy a file, start a service.
running twice changes nothing the second time.
a YAML file that strings modules together.
you can re-run a playbook safely at any time.
concepts.remember: Modules do one job and are idempotent — running the same playbook twice is safe.

concepts.title: Installing Ansible
concepts.main: Ansible comes from the AppStream repository and runs only on a Linux or UNIX control node.
simple: Windows is not supported as a control node — a genuine limitation worth knowing before you plan an architecture around it.
It is in the repositories on a default RHEL install, so no extra repository setup is needed.
parts: confirm the version and which Python it is using.
the control node cannot be Windows.
must be able to be reached over SSH.
concepts.remember: dnf install ansible from AppStream; the control node cannot be Windows.

concepts.title: The static inventory
concepts.main: The inventory is the list of machines Ansible knows about, usually grouped into named groups.
simple: A plain list of hostnames works for a small setup. Groups matter because they let one playbook target 'all webservers' rather than naming each one.
The group name is what you write in the hosts: line.
parts: variables applied to just that group.
Ansible can also refer to a host by IP if the name will not resolve.
concepts.remember: The inventory is a list of hosts in named groups — the group name is what you target in a play.

concepts.title: ansible.cfg search order
concepts.main: Ansible uses the first ansible.cfg it finds, in a fixed order of precedence.
simple: When your settings seem to be ignored, it is usually because a different ansible.cfg is winning.
The order is worth knowing precisely because it is a common exam question and a common real-world confusion.
parts: in the directory you run from.
shows which config file is actually in use.
concepts.remember: ANSIBLE_CONFIG beats ./ansible.cfg, which beats ~/.ansible.cfg, which beats /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg.

concepts.title: Ad hoc commands
concepts.main: An ad hoc command runs one module against some hosts, right now, without saving anything.
simple: The automation equivalent of typing a command by hand — but you can point it at fifty hosts at once.
They are for one-off checks and quick actions. Anything you will do again belongs in a playbook.
parts: the arguments to that module, in quotes.
concepts.remember: ansible <hosts> -m <module> -a 'args' — great for a one-off, wrong for anything repeatable.

concepts.title: module versus module arguments
concepts.main: The -m value is the module name; the -a value is the arguments, and the two are not interchangeable.
simple: A common mistake is putting the whole specification into -m. The module is just the tool's name; the arguments describe the job.
For modules that need nothing beyond the host list — like ping — no -a is required at all.
concepts.remember: -m is the module name only; arguments go in -a as key=value pairs.

chapters.inOneSentence: One control node drives many managed nodes over SSH with nothing installed on them; the inventory is named groups; and ad hoc commands are for one-offs while anything repeatable becomes a playbook.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III
chapters.title: Writing and Running Playbooks
chapters.partTitle: Part 2 — playbooks, multiple plays, privilege, variables, Vault and facts
chapters.source: RH294 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III)

concepts.title: The three levels
concepts.main: A playbook contains plays, a play contains tasks, and a task calls a module.
simple: The nesting is strict and the indentation must match it, because YAML uses indentation to mean structure.
Get the indentation wrong and you get a confusing error rather than an obvious one — so check the spaces before blaming the content.
parts: a play — one group of hosts with a set of tasks.
concepts.remember: playbook > plays > tasks > module — and YAML indentation is what defines those levels.

concepts.title: Running and checking a playbook
concepts.main: ansible-playbook runs it; --syntax-check and --check let you find mistakes without changing anything.
simple: Checking first costs seconds and turns a half-applied change into a clean error message.
--check is a dry run: it reports what it would do without touching the hosts.
parts: parse and report YAML errors without running.
dry run — report changes without making them.
restrict to specific hosts or a group.
concepts.remember: --syntax-check finds YAML errors; --check shows what would change without doing it.

concepts.title: Multiple plays and privilege escalation
concepts.main: One playbook can hold several plays targeting different groups, and each play can set its own become settings.
simple: This is what lets you configure a whole tier — load balancers, then web servers, then databases — in a single run, in the right order.
become gives you a root shell for the tasks that need one, without making the whole playbook root.
parts: run these tasks as root via sudo.
sudo is the default; su is the alternative.
escalate to a different user than the login user.
each with its own hosts — they run in order.
the fully qualified module name; the short form also works.
concepts.remember: Multiple plays run in order and each can set its own become: yes for the tasks that need root.

concepts.title: Naming and precedence
concepts.main: Variable names are strict, and several sources can define the same name — so precedence decides which wins.
simple: Precedence is how Ansible stays flexible: you can set a default in the playbook and override it per host when you need to.
It is also how a playbook stops behaving the way you expect if something higher up is overriding you.
parts: must start with a letter; letters, numbers and underscores only.
per host or per group, above inventory.
highest — overrides everything, for one run.
concepts.remember: Defaults are lowest and -e extra vars are highest — extra vars beat everything.

concepts.title: Precedence and registers
concepts.main: register saves a task's output into a variable, so later tasks can use it.
simple: It is how you ask a question and then act on the answer — check whether something is true, and only then do the change.
A registered variable is a dictionary, so you pull the interesting part out of it rather than using it directly.
example: - name: Check if nginx is installed
parts: capture this task's result into VAR.
keep going instead of aborting when this task fails.
concepts.remember: register captures a task's output; VAR.rc is the exit code and VAR.stdout the text.

concepts.title: Ansible Vault
concepts.main: Vault encrypts secrets inside a playbook or variables file so they can be stored safely.
simple: Passwords and API keys cannot live in a shared repository in plain text. Vault lets you keep them encrypted and still version-control the file.
The encrypted string is one long blob beginning with $ANSIBLE_VAULT.
parts: make or change an encrypted file.
encrypt a plain file in place.
supply the vault password at run time.
read the password from a file instead.
encrypt one value, for use inline in a playbook.
the vault password is the only thing protecting the secrets.
concepts.remember: Vault encrypts secrets so the file can be committed — but the vault password itself must never be committed.

concepts.title: What facts are and why they matter
concepts.main: Facts are variables Ansible discovers automatically about each managed host.
simple: Before it changes anything, Ansible asks each host to describe itself: its OS, kernel, memory, network interfaces, and whether it is a container.
That is how one playbook can configure Ubuntu and RHEL correctly — it does not have to be told which is which.
parts: the OS family — RedHat, Debian, Ubuntu.
skip fact gathering when you do not need it — much faster.
concepts.remember: Facts are auto-discovered facts about each host, and gather_facts: no skips the cost when you do not need them.

concepts.title: Gathering facts faster
concepts.main: Fact gathering is the slowest part of a short playbook, so turn it off when nothing uses the facts.
simple: For a playbook that only copies a file, asking every host to describe itself is pure overhead.
This is a real optimisation, not a micro-detail: it is often the difference between a fast run and a slow one across many hosts.
parts: at play level — skip gathering for this play.
run manually if you need just some facts.
facts you tell Ansible to remember, speeding later runs.
set once in ansible.cfg to turn it off globally.
concepts.remember: gather_facts: no at play level — worth it whenever no task uses a fact.

chapters.inOneSentence: A playbook nests plays, tasks and modules; become: yes escalates per play; register captures output for later tasks; -e beats everything; and gather_facts: no skips needless work.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III
chapters.title: Loops, Conditionals, Handlers and Failure Handling
chapters.partTitle: Part 3 — iteration, conditions, reacting to change, and error control
chapters.source: RH294 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III)

concepts.title: The loop keyword
concepts.main: loop runs one task once for every item in a list, instead of repeating the task by hand.
simple: Same idea as the shell for loop: describe the work once and let Ansible repeat it.
It is the difference between a five-line playbook and a fifty-line one.
parts: a list — each item runs the task once.
the current element; the name changes with loop_var.
rename item if you prefer something clearer.
the older syntax — still works, but loop is current.
concepts.remember: loop runs one task per list item; the element is {{ item }} unless you rename it.

concepts.title: The when conditional
concepts.main: when runs a task only if its condition is true.
simple: This is how a playbook adapts to what it finds — install the package only on the right OS family, copy the file only if it differs.
Conditions can test variables, registered results, or facts.
example: - name: Install httpd only on RHEL
parts: a bare dash means the condition failed and the task was skipped.
concepts.remember: when: gates a task on a condition; a skipped task is shown with a dash, not reported as a failure.

concepts.title: Multiple conditions and complex tests
concepts.main: Conditions combine with and, or, not — and grouping parentheses around them.
simple: Read it as you would a sentence: 'this and that, or the other thing'.
Without the parentheses, and binds tighter than or and you get a different meaning than you intended.
example: when: (a == 1 or b == 2) and not c
parts: several conditions, all must be true (AND).
group explicitly when mixing and with or.
Jinja syntax is implied in when.
concepts.remember: A list of conditions is AND; use and/or/not with parentheses when you need grouping.

concepts.title: What a handler does
concepts.main: A handler is a task that runs only when a task before it reported a change.
simple: The pattern is: update a config file, then restart the service — but only if the file actually changed.
Running the restart unconditionally wastes time on every host that did not change, and briefly drops service for no reason.
parts: call a handler if this task reports changed.
a section at play or playbook level.
a handler that is notified but not needed does nothing.
several handlers can share one notify name.
handlers run at the END of the play, not immediately.
concepts.remember: notify: calls a handler, which runs only on change — and at the end of the play, not straight away.

concepts.title: What happens when a task fails
concepts.main: By default a failed task aborts the remaining tasks for that host — but not for other hosts.
simple: Each host is independent. If one of fifty servers fails a task, the other forty-nine carry on. That is usually what you want.
This is worth understanding because it means a partial run is normal, and re-running is safe.
parts: later tasks for that host are skipped.
keep going on this host despite the failure.
decide yourself what counts as a failure.
report the task as ok even if it technically ran a command.
concepts.remember: A failure stops tasks for THAT host only; other hosts carry on.

concepts.title: ignore_errors, failed_when and failed_when conditions
concepts.main: ignore_errors swallows a failure; failed_when changes what counts as a failure.
simple: These are different tools for different situations, and confusing them causes real problems.
ignore_errors hides a genuine problem as much as it lets you continue. Use it when a failure genuinely does not matter.
failed_when lets a command that exits non-zero be treated as fine when you know the exit code is not a problem.
example: - name: Command that may exit non-zero harmlessly
parts: carry on past a failure — it is still reported as failed.
treat as failed only if your own condition holds.
never fail this task, whatever the exit code.
suppress the 'changed' report when nothing really changed.
add check_mode: false to let a task run under --check.
concepts.remember: ignore_errors continues past a failure; failed_when decides what counts as one; changed_when controls the 'changed' report.

chapters.inOneSentence: loop repeats a task per item and when gates it on a condition; notify triggers a handler only when something actually changed; and a failure stops only that host.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III
chapters.title: Managing Files and Jinja2 Templates
chapters.partTitle: Part 4 — file modules, templates, loops in templates, filters and tests
chapters.exam: RHCE (EX294) — 4.1-4.2 managing files and using templates
chapters.source: RH294 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III)

concepts.title: Choosing the right file module
concepts.main: Different modules handle different file needs — copying content, writing content, or only managing attributes.
simple: Reaching for the wrong one causes surprising behaviour: copy fails on a remote source, blockinfile duplicates entries, and lineinfile replaces the whole file.
parts: copy a file from the control node — src must be local.
write literal text instead of a file.
render a Jinja2 template from the control node.
create/delete/touch, and manage mode, owner, SELinux context.
insert a marked block, replacing it if present.
get a file FROM the managed node.
concepts.remember: copy and template move files from the control node; file manages attributes; lineinfile and blockinfile edit in place.

concepts.title: The file module for attributes only
concepts.main: The file module changes permissions, ownership and SELinux context without touching content.
simple: When a task's only job is to make a file's permissions correct, do not copy the file again — use the file module.
This is also the safe way to recursively fix a whole tree's ownership.
parts: create it, or update its timestamp if it exists.
permissions, best in quotes — 0755 can be read as octal.
concepts.remember: state: absent for deletion, touch to create, and always quote mode so it stays octal.

concepts.title: What a template does
concepts.main: A template is a source file with placeholders that Ansible fills in per host at deploy time.
simple: One config file works everywhere because the parts that differ — hostnames, addresses, versions — are substituted from that host's own facts and variables.
Without this you would need one config file per server, and they would drift apart immediately.
parts: a statement — a loop or a condition.
a comment that never reaches the output.
concepts.remember: {{ }} outputs a value, {% %} runs a statement, and {# #} is a template-only comment.

concepts.title: Loops and conditionals inside templates
concepts.main: Jinja2 supports for-loops and if-statements, with their own end tags.
simple: This is how one template produces a config containing a different number of entries depending on the host — servers, aliases, backends.
Every opening block needs a matching end, or the render fails with a confusing error.
parts: a host group from the inventory, as a list.
concepts.remember: {% for %}...{% endfor %} and {% if %}...{% endif %} — every opening block needs its end tag.

concepts.title: Filters and tests
concepts.main: A filter transforms a value's output; a test asks a yes/no question about it.
simple: Filters are like formatting — they change how a value appears without changing what it is.
Tests are different: they return true or false, and you use them inside a condition.
example: {% if var is defined %}   {% if var is number %}
parts: pipe a value through a transformation.
turn a list into a string.
use x if the value is undefined or empty.
concepts.remember: A filter transforms (| upper); a test asks a question (is defined) and returns true or false.

revision: file module: state, mode, owner, recurse
chapters.inOneSentence: Pick the file module that matches the job; templates fill in per-host values; {% %} blocks need their end tags; and filters transform values while tests return true or false.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III
chapters.title: Host Patterns, Dynamic Inventories and File Organisation
chapters.partTitle: Part 5 — targeting hosts, dynamic inventory, forks, and include versus import
chapters.exam: RHCE (EX294) — 5.1-5.4 inventory management and playbook organisation
chapters.source: RH294 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III)

concepts.title: The hosts: line is a pattern language
concepts.main: hosts: accepts far more than one group name — it is a full pattern language.
simple: Once you know the patterns you can express 'every web server except the one being rebuilt' in a single line.
This is what keeps playbooks readable instead of full of hand-written host lists.
parts: hosts in the group EXCEPT those in other (difference).
concepts.remember: hosts: uses a pattern language: & intersection, ! difference, * wildcard.

concepts.title: Why the inventory moves
concepts.main: A static file breaks down when machines are created and destroyed automatically — which is exactly how cloud works.
simple: If your servers come and go from a cloud provider, asking the cloud what exists right now is always correct and a typed file never is.
A dynamic inventory is a script that produces the inventory on demand.
parts: a file you maintain by hand.
a script that returns the host list.
show what Ansible actually resolved — the best debugging tool here.
output plain JSON or YAML and it is used directly.
cloud providers ship as plugins needing no script of your own.
concepts.remember: Dynamic inventory asks the environment what exists now; ansible-inventory --graph shows what Ansible actually resolved.

concepts.title: The forks setting
concepts.main: Forks controls how many managed hosts Ansible talks to at the same time.
simple: By default it is five. Raise it and a run across fifty machines finishes much faster — until you overload the control node or the target API.
It is a balance, and the limit is usually the control node's own capacity.
parts: faster, but can overload the control node or an API.
a different limit — process only this many hosts before moving on.
concepts.remember: Forks default to 5; raise with -f to speed up large runs, within what your control node can handle.

concepts.title: The difference that matters
concepts.main: import_* is processed when the playbook is parsed; include_* is processed when the play runs.
simple: Everything inside an imported file is known up front, so loops and conditionals around the import control whether it is loaded at all.
Included content is loaded as the play runs, so it can be used with tags, and each include may be evaluated separately.
example: - import_playbook: other.yml    # parsed now, must exist
- include_tasks: common.yml     # loaded at run time, can be conditional
parts: another playbook, parsed at parse time.
tasks or a role, parsed at parse time.
loaded at run time — works with tags and dynamic loops.
it is not a task, so it cannot take a loop.
a key reason to use include rather than import.
concepts.remember: import is parsed up front and must exist; include is loaded at run time, which is why it works with tags and loops.

concepts.title: Structuring a growing project
concepts.main: As a playbook grows, split it into a directory with inventories, roles and group variables.
simple: Keep each playbook focused on one concern and put shared setup in group_vars so it is not repeated.
The goal is that a new host is added by adding a line to an inventory, not by editing playbooks.
parts: variables for a group, loaded automatically.
variables for one host, loaded automatically.
concepts.remember: group_vars and host_vars load automatically by filename — that is how you avoid editing playbooks to add a host.

chapters.inOneSentence: hosts: is a pattern language using & ! and *; a dynamic inventory asks the environment what exists; forks defaults to 5; and import is parsed up front while include is loaded at run time.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III
chapters.title: Roles and Reusable Content
chapters.partTitle: Part 6 — role structure, RHEL System Roles, writing your own, and Galaxy
chapters.source: RH294 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III)

concepts.title: What a role is
concepts.main: A role is a standard directory layout that bundles everything one piece of functionality needs.
simple: Think of it as a box that already has labelled compartments: tasks in one, templates in another, defaults in a third.
Because the layout is standardised, Ansible finds everything without you telling it where anything is.
parts: variables that override anything — use sparingly.
concepts.remember: tasks/main.yml is required; defaults are lowest precedence; templates, handlers, files and meta are the other standard folders.

concepts.title: The directory search path
concepts.main: Ansible looks for a role in several places, in a fixed order.
simple: This is why the same role name behaves consistently regardless of where you run the playbook from.
Knowing the order explains why one copy is being used and not the other.
parts: shipped with packages — where RHEL System Roles live.
concepts.remember: Role search order: playbook's roles/, /etc/ansible/roles, ~/.ansible/roles, then /usr/share/ansible/roles.

concepts.title: What they are
concepts.main: RHEL System Roles are Red Hat-provided and Red Hat-SUPPORTED roles for common subsystems.
simple: They exist so you do not have to write a role for SELinux, firewall, Apache or storage yourself.
The supported part matters: if one breaks, Red Hat is accountable for it. A community role from Galaxy is not.
parts: packaged as ordinary RPMs — installed with dnf.
they come from the official repositories.
concepts.remember: RHEL System Roles are packaged as ansible-role-redhat-* RPMs — dnf install, no Galaxy required.

concepts.title: Scaffolding and using your own role
concepts.main: ansible-galaxy init builds the standard skeleton, and you then fill in the tasks.
simple: The command creates every folder Ansible expects, so you are not guessing the layout.
Then reference the role by name in a play — or in a roles/ directory beside your playbook.
parts: use it in a play's roles: section.
concepts.remember: ansible-galaxy init builds the skeleton; then reference the role by name in the roles: section.

concepts.title: Ansible Galaxy
concepts.main: Galaxy is a public hub of community-contributed roles, installable by name.
simple: It saves writing something that already exists. But community roles carry no Red Hat support and you are trusting a stranger's code.
Read a role before you run it in production — it is code from the internet.
parts: roles_path controls where they are installed.
community code — review before running it.
concepts.remember: Galaxy saves writing roles that exist, but they are community code with no Red Hat support — read before you trust it.

chapters.inOneSentence: A role is a standard folder layout with tasks, defaults, templates and handlers; RHEL System Roles are supported RPMs you install with dnf; and Galaxy roles are community code worth reading first.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III
chapters.title: Troubleshooting Playbooks and Managed Hosts
chapters.partTitle: Part 7 — logging playbook output, debugging, and fixing managed nodes
chapters.source: RH294 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III)

concepts.title: Ansible logs nothing by default
concepts.main: Without configuration, Ansible's output goes only to the terminal and is never written to a file.
simple: So when a run fails at 2am, there is nothing to look back at. Turning on logging first is what makes any future failure investigable.
parts: where the log file is written.
very verbose — includes module arguments and results.
capture stderr, where the detail lives.
increase verbosity on the command line.
ANSIBLE_DEBUG is very noisy — use it when something is genuinely wrong.
concepts.remember: Nothing is logged unless you set ANSIBLE_LOG_PATH; use -v to -vvvv to raise verbosity.

concepts.title: Syntax check, check mode and diff
concepts.main: Three separate levels of safety exist before you let a playbook change anything.
simple: --syntax-check parses without running. --check runs the logic but makes no changes. --diff shows exactly what would change.
Use all three before a first run against anything important.
parts: YAML and structure errors only. Instant.
runs modules in check mode — no changes made.
show the before/after diff for changed files.
the safest way to preview a run.
opt a specific task out so it really runs.
concepts.remember: --syntax-check parses, --check changes nothing, --diff shows what would change.

concepts.title: Reading the recap line
concepts.main: The recap at the end tells you exactly what happened across every host.
simple: ok is unchanged, changed is a modification, unreachable is a connectivity problem, failed is a task that errored.
When a run does not do what you expected, this line is usually where the answer is.
parts: tasks that succeeded with no change.
could not connect — SSH or connectivity problem.
concepts.remember: The PLAY RECAP tells you ok, changed, unreachable, failed and skipped per host — read it first.

concepts.title: Modules that ignore check mode
concepts.main: command, shell and script always run, even under --check.
simple: Ansible cannot know what a raw command will do, so it runs it. That means a --check run can still change things — which defeats the point.
Use changed_when: false and failed_when: false to control how those are reported.
parts: the opposite — force a task to skip in check mode.
concepts.remember: command, shell and script run even under --check — pair them with changed_when and failed_when.
concepts.warning: A --check run is not always harmless. command, shell and script still execute, so anything that changes state can still change it.

concepts.title: The unreachable problem
concepts.main: When Ansible cannot reach a host, almost every cause is SSH or credentials.
simple: Work through it in order: can you ssh in by hand? Does the key exist with correct permissions? Is the inventory right? Is it a first-boot prompt?
ansible -m ping is the fastest way to isolate connectivity from playbook problems.
parts: the first thing to run — isolates connectivity.
if that fails, it is not an Ansible problem.
SSH refuses until the host key is accepted — visible as a timeout.
-K prompts once instead of per host.
the remote account is missing or locked.
concepts.remember: Start with ansible -m ping — if plain ssh fails too, it is never an Ansible problem.
concepts.warning: An unreachable host after a fresh install is usually SSH waiting on a first-connection host key prompt.

concepts.title: Module failure versus task failure
concepts.main: A module can fail because the software is missing, the package name is wrong, or the service is not installed yet.
simple: The error text usually says which. Read it before changing the playbook — often the module is right and the machine is not ready.
Ordering tasks so a package is installed before it is configured prevents most of this.
parts: the named module does not exist — check the spelling.
configure before installing. Reorder the tasks.
the error usually names what was not found.
most failures of this kind are just tasks in the wrong order.
concepts.remember: Module failure is often the machine not being ready, not the module being wrong — install before you configure.

chapters.inOneSentence: Nothing is logged until you set ANSIBLE_LOG_PATH; --syntax-check, --check and --diff are your three safety levels; and an unreachable host is almost always SSH rather than Ansible.

chapters.bookTitle: Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III
chapters.title: Automating Core Administration
chapters.partTitle: Part 8 — packages, users, scheduling, storage and networking, all as modules
chapters.source: RH294 course material (Red Hat Enterprise Linux Administration III)

concepts.title: Managing software
concepts.main: The package module makes package management declarative rather than a sequence of commands.
simple: Instead of 'install it and hope', you state the desired state and Ansible works out whether anything needs doing.
That is what makes it idempotent — and why re-running is safe.
parts: also upgraded to the newest available.
concepts.remember: dnf module: state present installs, latest also upgrades, absent removes.

concepts.title: Managing users
concepts.main: The user and group modules declare accounts and memberships declaratively.
simple: Append to a group rather than replace, so the module does not silently strip the memberships you did not mention — the usermod -a trap in module form.
parts: ADD to groups, not replace them.
set it — prefer password_hash with a hash.
concepts.remember: append: yes adds to supplementary groups instead of replacing them.
concepts.warning: Without append: yes, specifying groups replaces the account's existing supplementary groups.

concepts.title: Scheduling with modules
concepts.main: The at and cron modules automate one-time and recurring scheduling.
simple: The RHEL 8-era shell wrappers like at and cron are available as modules, so the same thing you did by hand in RH134 now becomes a task.
This is the practical payoff of having learned the commands first.
example: - name: Remove a user in five minutes
parts: recurring jobs — minute, hour, day, month, weekday, job.
reboot, yearly, hourly, daily — same names as in a crontab.
concepts.remember: The at module does one-time jobs and cron does recurring ones — same concepts as RH134, now declarative.

concepts.title: Managing storage
concepts.main: The storage stack — partition, PV, VG, LV, filesystem, mount — maps onto modules one for one.
simple: What you learned as a manual order in RH134 becomes a list of tasks in the same order.
The ordering matters just as much: a filesystem task before its volume exists will fail.
parts: create a filesystem on a device.

concepts.main: RH124 teaches you to run systems, RH134 teaches you to automate and secure them, RH294 scales both across many hosts.
simple: Each course assumes the one before. That is why RH294 opens by assuming you are already comfortable with systemd, storage and SELinux.
